Live Science spoke with marine biologist Annie Mercier about her role as a science adviser for Netflix's show "Below."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In Netflix's new series "Below," an ancient, squid-like creature known as "Mudder" threatens a small coastal community in Newfoundland, Canada, arriving around the same time as a mysterious iceberg that starts causing dangerous hallucinations in the town's residents.

The series blends marine science, horror and environmental themes, harking back to Newfoundland's long-standing connections with giant squid (Architeuthis dux), with the first sightings going back to the 1870s.

Annie Mercier, a marine biologist in the Department of Ocean Sciences at Memorial University in Newfoundland and Labrador, was brought on as a science adviser in 2025 just before Netflix began shooting "Below." Mercier's research focuses on deep sea organisms, studying their behavior, interactions and how they respond to environmental stressors like climate change.

Mercier's lab at the Ocean Sciences Center was used as a filming location, and she met with actor Mackenzie Davis, who plays the research scientist Dr. Fonda Howander, to guide the character. Live Science spoke with Mercier about how she helped bring Mudder — and the scientific endeavour to unravel its mystery — to life.

Annie Mercier is a professor in the Department of Ocean Sciences at Memorial University inNewfoundland and Labrador, Canada. She studies marine animals and their response to environmental conditions, conducting research on the behaviors and interactions of diverse invertebrate species from Arctic and deep-sea environments.

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry: How did you end up getting involved with "Below" as a scientific adviser?

Annie Mercier: Early in 2025, when they were just about to start filming or were finalizing the scripts, I heard that Jesse Mckeown [the director] was looking for a scientific adviser, preferably someone here in Newfoundland. We heard about it through Memorial University's communications team. They mentioned that there would be something about an ancient cephalopod in the series.

I'm not an expert in cephalopods … But I do have a broad background in marine biology, and I'm here at the Ocean Sciences Centre. I sent back my reply, and they eventually contacted me to ask more about what I was doing and what I'd worked on in the past. My research is centered around strange creatures and trying to understand them through curiosity-driven research, so I guess that resonated with them.

Another factor was that I'd previously worked as a consultant on documentaries and television series. I'd done a little work with the BBC, helping explain video sequences, as well as fiction series back in Quebec. I also write popular articles and books for general audiences, so I'm familiar with navigating between science and fiction and with trying to convey something wonderful about science in language that general audiences can understand. I guess that played a role as well, and they eventually asked me to be the adviser.

A view of the Ocean Sciences Center where Mercier works.

KHC: What did the advising process look like?

This article is part of a series called "Science Behind the Camera," which focuses on the role of science advisers in popular science and films . From helping to create engaging stories to designing sets and advising on scripts, these experts shape some of the most compelling narratives on screen.

AM: There were two phases. The main thing was that they wanted to share the scripts early on. That's when I was brought in.

Jesse told me they would send scripts at regular intervals, in sequence, starting with the first episode, then the second, and so forth. They would securely send me each script. We had some preliminary discussions to establish exactly what they wanted, because that was my question: How much detail or what kind of feedback were they looking for?

They told me that whatever came to mind, I should suggest it. Of course, I knew they couldn't take everything into account, but I think they wanted to know how far-fetched or how close to reality some of the things were. They asked me to focus mostly on the scientific aspects.

That included the squid, but also how they portrayed the scientific work and the character involved in it. They had climate change, icebergs, ocean currents and a number of other scientific elements in the story.

I went through every script and provided feedback on all sorts of things. Sometimes it was something as simple as the timing of an event. I pointed out things related to the migrations of marine animals and other details that I knew were a little different from reality.

I provided written feedback and sometimes links to additional information. I'd send it back, and occasionally there would be a follow-up meeting or a remote conversation about certain elements. It depended on the situation.

When they started filming, Jesse wanted to schedule a time for me to go behind the scenes and chat with the crew. It was difficult to coordinate because they were filming on three or more sets around Newfoundland, and I was working. Eventually, I managed to visit on a Saturday when they were filming at the Ocean Sciences Centre. I spent some time in the control room, met Mackenzie [Davis] and got to see what they were doing on-site.

Of course, when you're asked about giant squids and you know it's a fictional show, all sorts of things come to mind.

KHC: How much feedback did you end up giving on Mudder, the giant, squid-like creature? What aspects did you think were accurate, and where did the show take creative liberties?

AM: Of course, when you're asked about giant squids and you know it's a fictional show, all sorts of things come to mind. I was hoping they wouldn't go the route of having the arms come out and a giant squid jump onto a boat, or something like "20,000 Leagues Under the Sea." You see those kinds of things in some of the drawings from the 1800s, too. So I had some fears about that.

But when I read the scripts, I could see they were trying to make it as close to reality as possible. Obviously, they had some freedom because it's portrayed as an ancient, social type of cephalopod — more like a squid but with some octopus-like behaviors as well.

I focused my feedback on biology. For example, the eye was very large. It's well known that existing giant squids have one of the biggest, if not the biggest, eyes in the animal kingdom. So that was definitely something that made sense.

A drawing of a giant squid from the Connecticut Academy of Sciences dating to between 1879 and 1881. The drawing shows the large eye of the giant squid.

I also cautioned them about how giant squids move. Sometimes, in movies, you see their arms portrayed as very muscular, reaching far out of the water. These are mollusks [cephalopods belong to the phylum Mollusca], and in the water, they have quite a bit of strength. But outside the water, they don't have bones that attach muscles to support that kind of movement. It's a very different type of movement.

I drew their attention to the very few cephalopods that actually go out of the water. There's an octopus you can see on certain reefs, and I sent them some images of it. I explained that its movement is very fluid, the way it's able to advance across reefs outside the water.

I also mentioned the kinds of scars they could leave when interacting with sperm whales, for example.

I was quite happy to see that they kept the creature rather mysterious instead of trying to show too much. I was worried it might look completely funny, but I thought they made good use of keeping the mystery alive for a long time.

I also explained that cephalopods in the ocean have no way of detecting prey on the shore. They can't see it or sense it. So if you're going in that direction, you need to be a little careful. Obviously, that's where we're getting into fiction.

But I think they handled it pretty well. An audience expects some fearsome interactions, and if you don't include those at all, you'll disappoint people. Overall, I thought it was pretty good.

There's a lot of lore surrounding giant squids in Newfoundland. They definitely go together ‪—‬ not just in fiction but also because there have been remains, sightings and other encounters. I think this physical place played a role in the inspiration for the show's topic.

KHC: Did you advise on the hallucinogenic properties of the creature's mucus?

AM: No, we didn't specifically exchange information about that. A lot of marine animals have toxins. That's well known, and it's not just cephalopods; all sorts of marine animals have them. Now, how something like that could become airborne, or how it could be associated with melting icebergs and then ingested through the ice, is definitely fictional.

I'm aware of toxic substances, but I'm not aware of any that produce hallucinations, per se. And again, I'm no expert in that area.

KHC: Overall, do you think the series did a good job portraying science? Was there anything you would have changed?

AM: As I said, I had some fears at first. One downside of being an adviser was that I knew everything about the show before watching it, which was a first for me. It was a little different because I would watch and think, "Oh, OK; they did that. They adjusted this. Oh, they went all out with this one."

I discovered what they had taken into consideration and what they had discarded. It was fun to watch, and I think they did a pretty good job overall.

I always think about this when I watch series about different professions. When you see lawyers or police officers portrayed, I imagine they're probably laughing about how simple things seem. Maybe everything is compressed in time, or maybe it's not quite how it happens in reality. This time, it was my turn to see how they would portray my profession.

Mackenzie Davis, as Dr. Fonda Howander, conveys much of the science around giant squids in "Below."

I think they avoided some of the common clichés. In movies and television, when you go into a laboratory, you often see colorful tubes and bubbling Erlenmeyer flasks just to tell you that you're in a lab. The fact that they filmed here at the Ocean Sciences Centre, in real laboratories, contributed to the sense of reality. Our labs are eclectic. You have nets, tanks, microscopes and all sorts of things around. They're not perfectly ordered, and I think that helped.

I also appreciated that they were careful about how they portrayed scientists. When you're a marine scientist, you're a marine scientist. You're not all-knowing about everything in science. Sometimes shows portray scientists as knowing everything about everything.

For example, when it came to the substance in the show and its effects on health, I explained that a marine scientist might know how to make a diagnosis about something, but that doesn't mean they can necessarily provide a medical assessment. I think the character even says, "I'm not a medical doctor."

I also thought they did a good job portraying scientific uncertainty. In science, you follow lines of inquiry, but you're not necessarily sure what the answer is. You need confirmation and further investigation.

They also did what they could with the squid to make it fearsome but also lovable, without going too far from what a squid might actually do. And when they took creative liberties, they kept things mysterious enough that everything wasn't spelled out exactly.

I also thought they did a great job portraying Newfoundland. They captured the landscapes, the environments and the spirit of the people. The atmosphere was really well done. I think they aimed to make Newfoundland almost a character in the series, and they did that quite well.

Altogether, I thought the Ocean Sciences Centre and the labs were portrayed very nicely. Some of the students here were around during filming in 2025, and they've had showings of the episodes at the university. It's nice for them to see the labs where they work every day portrayed on screen.

Josh Harnett's character Calvin Penney relies on Mackenzie Davis's character Dr. Fonda Howander to learn more about the science of giant squids.

KHC: Beyond the creature itself, were there other scientific details in the scripts that you helped the writers get right?

AM: Yes. I provided feedback on a lot of smaller issues, including the use of scientific tools and how different analyses work.

For example, they were trying to date a block of ice. The process was a little different in the original script, and I explained that these analyses take time. You don't just do something in a lab and immediately get an answer. You sometimes have to collaborate with other people to establish things.

I also cautioned against making one microscope tell you everything about something you're looking at. A microscope is there to provide good magnification. It doesn't give you chemical signatures or anything like that. So I tried to caution them against making one instrument do more than it actually does in reality.

I thought they treated the laboratory work quite well overall. One thing they kept ‪—‬ and I can't blame them for it ‪—‬ was the very nice, almost magical tool they use to check the quality of icebergs. You just stick it into the iceberg, get a reading, and it tells you whether it's a good-quality iceberg.

Obviously, when I saw that, I thought it would be nice if it worked that way! But when you want to know the quality of ice or water, there are a number of different analyses you need to do, and you need to know what you're looking for.

In movies and television, it's often the case that you put something into a machine and it spits out exactly what you want to know. But in real science, you have to ask the right question. You have to know what you're looking for so the instrument can tell you whether something has a particular property or not.

I understood that they sometimes needed to take creative liberties to move the plot along. There were a number of comments I made about basic science and what was or wasn't realistic.

One feature of the Ocean Sciences Centre that they took into the fictional realm was the basement, where you go through a door and there's an ocean or water behind it. Obviously, don't look for that here! That's just about the only thing that isn't real. The rest is pretty close to reality.

Editor's note: This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

Kenna is also a book author, with her upcoming book 'Octopus X' scheduled for release in spring of 2027. Her beats include physics, health, environmental science, technology, AI, animal intelligence, corvids, and cephalopods.

#6385. A New Discovery is Re-Drawing the Map of the Milky Way

Star formation is a galaxy's foundational process. Astronomers study how star-forming gas moves around in a galaxy, where it's compressed, and in which parts of a galaxy stars form. In a barred spiral galaxy like the Milky Way, star formation is mostly concentrated in the spiral arms. In the central bar, star formation is more sluggish.

Recent research shows that though the central bar contains many stars, star formation there is mostly concentrated in the bar ends. Shear forces, streaming motions, and overpowering shocks that make the gas in the bars turbulent all combine to to inhibit star formation.

The Milky Way is a typical barred spiral galaxy, and astronomers have studied it intently to understand where star formation is concentrated. There's ongoing scientific debate about what happens in a barred spiral galaxy's central bar. Observations of other spiral barred galaxies show that star formation suppression there isn't necessarily universal. Part of the difficulty in understanding our own galaxy is observing the region. Since we're embedded in the galaxy, it's difficult to observe the bar. In many ways, astronomers have an easier time observing other galaxies.

Researchers from Australia and Sweden have found an unusual structure in the Milky Way's center that appears to set it apart from many other barred spiral galaxies. It's a vast collection of rotating stars in the central bar that's generating powerful and large shock fronts in the gas. These shock fronts are triggering star formation in the structure, which goes against the idea that stars can't form there.

The results are in new research titled "The nature of the Norma arm as a bar-driven star-forming shock front," and it's published in Nature Astronomy. The lead author is Dr. Hilary Davis from the University of Sydneyâs School of Physics and Sydney Institute for Astronomy. The research is casting doubt on the existence of one of the Milky Way's spiral arms, the Norma arm.

This illustration shows the Milky Way's major and minor spiral arms, as well as its central bar. The Norma arm is close to the galaxy's center. Image Credit: NASA.

"The Milky Way is commonly depicted as having four main spiral arms, including the Normaâouter arm, and a central stellar bar whose properties remain debated," the authors write. In past work, researchers have used astrophysical masers, which are coherent microwave emissions from young massive stars, to trace part of the Norma arm that extends from the central bar. So those results suggest that the masers reside along the Norma spiral arm.

But the Milky Way's bar is tricky to study. âThe Galactic bar cannot be easily observed because of a combination of our position in the Galaxy and dust obscuring our view,â Dr Davis said. âAs a result, the barâs properties have been highly debated.â

This new research, based on observations and massive astrophysical simulations suggests that what those masers really trace is the shock front or dust lane in its bar. Since stars form along shock fronts where gas is compressed, star formation is at the heart of this work. "This implies that the bar dust lane is star-forming, shedding new light on our understanding of star formation processes in the Milky Way," the authors explain.

This graphic shows modelling of the Milky Way with the Norma arm overlapping the bar shock front in the Milky Way. It's based on observations of masers from young stars. Previous research suggested those masers and young stars were in the Norma arm, but this work shows they're tracing star formation along a shock front in the Milky Way's central bar. Image Credit: Hillary Davis/University of Sydney

âAt its heart, star formation is a process we understand from everyday physics. Forces set matter in motion. In this case gas is compressed, and that compression can create the conditions for new stars to be born on a massive scale,â lead author Davis said.

Modern telescopes give us clear views of other galaxies on a regular basis. Observations of other spiral galaxies show that star formation is abundant in their spiral arms, where gas is compressed by density waves.

âIn most similar galaxies, star formation very commonly occurs along spiral arms. Whatâs extraordinary is seeing this happen in a different region of our Galaxy, where shocks are usually so strong that star formation is often suppressed,â said Davis.

The researchers used large-scale astrophysical models run on powerful computers to try to understand the masers and what they meant for star formation, and what part of the Milky Way's structure they traced. They found that the masers indicated star formation along a shock front in the bar, not in the Norma arm. Observational challenges made it seem like those masers were in the Norma arm.

âWe believe that the Milky Wayâs bar has star formation occurring along its shock front, which is uncommon for most bars in nearby galaxies,â Dr Davis said.

This figure from the research shows how what appears to be a spiral arm with star formation is actually the shock front from the central bar where stars are forming. "The red scatter points with black borders are the Norma masers," the authors write, but they actually line up with the shock front and may not be a spiral bar at all. Image Credit: Davis, H., Bland-Hawthorn, J., Tepper-GarcÃ­a, T. et al. The nature of the Norma arm as a bar-driven star-forming shock front. Nat Astron (2026).

"The Norma masers trace very young (âª1âMyr) star-forming regions that are still close to the gas clouds in which they formed because they have not had sufficient time to migrate away. Hence, the association of Norma masers with the Galactic bar shock front suggests that SF is occurring along the Galactic bar dust lane," the authors explain.

The result is that part of the Norma arm may have lost its status as a spiral arm.

âWe found that masers previously associated with the Norma arm closely align with the shock front predicted by our simulations,â Dr Davis said. âThis suggests that at least part of the so-called Norma arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a region of star formation along the leading edge of the Galactic bar."

These results show that stars can more readily form in the central bar, something that seemed prohibitive. âThis raises questions about the Galaxyâs spiral structure, and the bar region of the Milky Way, which needs further investigation,â she said.

Astronomers have studied the Milky Way's central bar and argued about its nature for decades. There's been plenty of uncertainty about its properties and its role in star formation, and these results are shaping our understanding of the bar. âOur findings place further constraints on the size, angle and rotation speed of this central bar,â Dr Davis said.

"By associating the masers with the simulated shock front, we determine the parameters of the bar to be: a â 4.3 Â± 0.2 kpc, b â 2.3 Â± 0.2 kpc, Ï = 20(+5/-2)âand Î©p â² 40 km sâ1 kpcâ1, representing the semimajor and semiminor half-lengths of the bar, the inclination angle and the pattern speed, respectively," the authors write.

In plain language, they're saying that the bar's full, end-to-end length is about 28,000 light years, its width is about 15,000 light years, and it's tilted about 20 degrees from our line of sight. It also takes about 154 million years to complete one rotation.

For comparison, prior estimates of the bar's length range from 3,000 to 16,000 light years, and its width has been estimated between 8,000 and 16,000 light years. Measurements of its time to complete one rotation range from 102 to 246 million years. So these results are inside existing ranges.

The wide ranges for its size and rotation speed illustrate how difficult studying the bar is. The wide ranges may seem absurd, but astronomers have had limited observations to work with. Overall, these results add new constraints on the bar's properties, and they carry more weight based on how the researchers arrived at them.

âBy comparing a new generation of large-scale computerised galaxy simulations, evolving over billions of years, against a more limited set of observations, we now have a stronger understanding of the bar and star formation processes in the Milky Way,â Dr Davis said.

The main finding is that the bar has the ability to form stars, and that may mean the Milky Way is different from many other barred spirals.

"This raises questions about the Milky Wayâs spiral structure and suggests that the Galactic bar is long, slow and star-forming," the authors write.

#6384. I’ve Tested Vacuums for Years. These Are the 6 Best Cordless Stick Vacs Under $300, Ranked.

Clean hardwood, carpet, pet hair, and everything in between for less.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The most powerful cordless stick vacuums will easily run you $500 or more, but in my experience, there are plenty of capable cleaners under $300. They may not rival the suction power, battery life, or features of their higher-priced counterparts, but many are perfectly capable of keeping up with typical household messes on hardwood, carpet, and every surface in between.

I’ve spent years testing vacuums for Popular Mechanics, and that experience informs a lot of my recommendations below. Some of these models have been through my own series of hands-on tests, while others made the cut based on my familiarity with their brands and product lines, along with research into their features and real-world performance. From budget-friendly everyday cleaners to options for pet owners, these are the best cordless vacuums that deliver the most for under $300.

The Shark PowerDetect is a feature-packed option for anyone who wants a cordless stick vacuum that does a lot of the thinking for them. The Detect mode automatically adjusts suction based on floor type and amount of debris, and a dual-roller floor head tackles tough messes on hardwood and carpet.

The hinged wand is great for cleaning under furniture and makes it a lot easier to reach hidden areas without having to bend down at all kinds of weird angles. It’s on the heavier side, and the long recharge time is a drawback, but strong pickup and smart features make it a good pick for whole-home cleaning.

Don’t let the price fool you: The Bissell PowerClean FurFinder is a strong and versatile cordless vacuum. It isn’t too heavy to carry between rooms, and the self-standing design means you don’t have to remount it or lay it flat any time you need to pause during your cleaning session.

It has a tangle-free brush roll that does a great job picking up pet hair (as well as your own stray strands around the house). I also like the LED headlights that show hidden dirt, dust, and debris on floors and furniture. The attachments are great for above-floor cleaning, too. Battery life drops considerably when you crank up the suction power, so it’s best for maintenance cleaning.

The LVAC-300 packs cleaning power and everyday convenience into a lightweight machine. It’s easy to maneuver, and it transitions between hard floors, rugs, and low- to medium-pile carpet without scattering debris all over the floor. The tangle-resistant brush roll is a major pro for homes with pets or long hair, and five-stage filtration and washable filters are valuable additions.

It converts to a handheld vacuum cleaner with attachments for upholstery, stairs, and car interiors, and it uses a pleated mechanical HEPA filter with a dense arrangement of fibers to capture even the tiniest dust particles. The smaller dustbin and shorter runtime on max power might negatively impact your overall experience using this vacuum, but still, it’s versatile enough to take care of a variety of common household messes.

The Tineco Pure One Station 5 is the sibling to the Station 5 Pro that I’ve tested and still use to this day. And luckily, this more affordable model doesn’t cut key features that I love, such as the self-emptying and self-cleaning bagless docking station and green laser light for dust detection.

This model also has HEPA filtration and smart features. Internal sensors detect dust and adjust suction accordingly, and the anti-tangle brush roll helps prevent hair buildup. You get a shorter runtime with this model than you do with the Pro (estimated 70 minutes compared to the Pro’s 100), but the automated cleaning capability is hard to beat.

The Dyson V8 is right at the edge of our $300 budget, but it’s a powerful option for homes with lots of carpeting or area rugs. I haven’t tried this specific model yet, but the motorbar floor cleaner is the same design that comes with other Dyson vacuums I’ve tried, such as the Dyson V15 Detect. It works well for hard floors, but I’ve found it particularly useful for dislodging embedded hair and debris from carpet fibers.

The V8 comes with three attachments and converts into a handheld vacuum if you need more portability. Runtime is on the lower end for Dyson, but if you’re looking for a premium design without the premium price tag, the V8 is it.

The Eureka ReactiSense 440 offers a number of features that make vacuuming less of a chore. It has dust detection sensors, automatic suction adjustment, floor head lights, and an anti-tangle brush roll with fins and a comb strip to prevent hair from getting wrapped around it.

I like that this model uses HEPA filtration to capture up to 99.7 percent of airborne particles and odors (which is great if you’re a pet owner). This model is lightweight and portable, converts to a handheld, and provides up to 60 minutes of runtime. Battery life will likely vary if you’re regularly cleaning at high power levels, but I’d reach for this vacuum for daily maintenance cleaning and quick pickups.

#6383. Using Lunar Craters as Free Radiation Shields for Moon Base Nuclear Reactors

Powering any future lunar base is a massive engineering challenge. The two-week lunar night can drain batteries charged by solar panels during the two-week day, if the batteries themselves can even withstand the freezing temperatures that go along with it. So, for decades at this point, engineers have planned to use a nuclear reactor to at least partially power any future human settlement on the Moon. A new paper from researchers at Los Alamos, NASA Glenn, Oak Ridge, Idaho National Lab, and Lockheed Martin, and presented at the American Nuclear Societyâs Nuclear and Emerging Technologies for Space (NETS) conference back in April, offers a simple solution to one major problem for any such future nuclear reactor - shielding.

Currently, space-based nuclear power is advancing under a NASA program known as the Space Power and Reactor Capabilities (SPARC) program. One crucial constraint in this plan to build a 40-kilowatt nuclear reactor on the Moon is its weight limit. Any system has to be under 6,000 kg in order to fit on a mobile rover on the lunar surface.

Thatâs not a lot of weight to work with for a nuclear reactor, especially one of that size. And in addition to being one of the most important health and safety parts of a reactor, shielding is also one of the heaviest. To lower the weight of their systems, space reactor designers have historically relied on directional âshadow shields.â Instead of encompassing an entire reactor with an absorbent material like lead or concrete, they use lightweight hydrogen-rich materials like lithium hydride combined with dense metal positioned in a specific direction to protect highly sensitive parts of the reactor itself, such as the control electronics.

Fraser talks in detail about the Kilopower reactor.

Directional shields mean the rest of the area around the reactor is left unprotected, which isnât great if part of that area is zoned for human habitation. Even 1 km away from the reactor site, the amount of radiation if left unprotected would be deadly. But bringing up even more shielding from Earth to protect any such habitation zone is extraordinarily expensive.

To solve this problem, the research team, led by Los Alamos researcher Alex Levinsky, turned to a simple solution â use natural lunar terrainâlike a crater depression or a dirt hillâto block the direct line of sight, and thereby most of the radiation from reaching the habitation area. Since building a mockup lunar nuclear reactor and procuring hundreds of tons of lunar regolith presumably wasnât in the budget for this research, the team turned to computer simulations instead.

They used a software called Monte Carlo N-Particle to simulate millions of subatomic particles emanating from the nuclear reactor core. Placing it 1.5 m off the ground allowed them to simulate its positioning on the back of a wheeled rover. They then started modeling what different kinds of barricades would look like between the reactor and the habitation space.

Fraser talks about lunar base site selection and why it needs a fission reactor.

First, their simulations focused on arbitrary landscapes, such as a three-meter-deep crater or a gently sloping three-meter-high dirt hill. Both effectively blocked almost all of the radiation coming from the reactor, knocking it down to roughly one-tenth of a rem per yearâabout fifty times lower than the five-rem-per-year limit set for reactor radiation above the Moon's natural background.

With that success in mind, the next task was to model an actual environment. The research team chose Connecting Ridge, a mountain ridge near Shackleton Crater at the Lunar South Pole. This is an ideal site for future crewed missions, as it combines two of the most sought-after features of the lunar landscape. Some of the ridges are in almost permanent sunlight, being lit 80-90% of the time, while also being right next to Permanently Shadowed Regions that never see the Sun at all and are home to deposits of water ice that is crucial to life support and rocketry in any future permanent colony.

When placing the reactor in this environment, the research team made sure to respect the limitations of the rover (no slopes more than 18 degrees), but managed to find a natural depression that could be separated from a simulated base camp by a 120-m-high crater wall. With that barrier in place, the radiation hitting the habitat from the reactor dropped to near zeroâonly about four-hundredths of a rem per yearâallowing the reactor's onboard shadow shield to focus solely on protecting nearby electronics.

Fraser talks about finding water ice in the Moon's Permanently Shadowed Craters.

One nice feature about the airless Moon in this context is the engineers donât have to deal with âskyshineâ â a phenomenon where radiation shot into the sky bounces off air particles there and bounces back down onto the habitat. Since the Moon has no atmosphere, there is nothing for the radiation to bounce off of, solving one of the problems with reactors on Earth.

However, there is one major catch. While placing regolith between the reactor and the habitat protects the habitat itself, inside the crater or operational space of the reactor is a death zone. Astronauts would immediately develop radiation poisoning if entering the area while the reactor is in operation. And since regolith actually reflects neutrons pretty well, many of those neutrons are reflected directly into space, meaning no spacecraft or landers could fly directly over it.

So while we might be able to save thousands of kilograms of launch cost by building our own radiation shields on the Moon, we might also create a no-fly exclusion zone on one particular part of the Moon, just to ensure that astronauts have light and heat during the long, cold lunar nights. That is likely a tradeoff many space enthusiasts will be willing to make. And this study will bring the dream of reliable, continuous nuclear power on our nearest celestial neighbor one step closer to reality.

#6382. 2026 Was the Year Restaurants Went Full Midwest

It’s a giardinera- and tavern-style-stuffed, totally welcoming time in hospitality

At Kyle Knall’s Milwaukee restaurant Cassis, the showstopper dish is ravioli Dauphiné, a sheet of 24 tiny squares stuffed with the Wisconsin cheese Pleasant Ridge Reserve. Topped with glazed seasonal veggies, kernels of sweet corn in summer and sliced honeynut squash in late fall, it speaks to Knall’s Midwestern-meets-French approach—one of the reasons why his restaurant earned a slot on Eater’s 2026 list of the Best New Restaurants in America.

The Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, feature serious Midwest representation. The Best New Restaurants list includes Chicago’s Creepies, which also digs into that Midwest-French mashup, and Kansas City’s Akoya Omakase, which brings a distinct viewpoint to the omakase experience. Meanwhile, the pickled walleye cheeks at Rosy in Cleveland and the puffed grain toast at All Well in Chicago are among the Restaurant Dishes of the Year, and Chicago’s Bad Butter, a place best-known for its croissant take on a Chicago-style hot dog, is one of the Best New Bakeries. It even includes drinks—Culebra, a Puerto Rican spot that draws on the Latinx influences of its Chicago neighborhood, is on Punch’s Best New Bars list. Between these accolades and other national recognition, all eyes are on the Midwest right now. And that’s even before we get into the impact of the Chicago-set show The Bear, which put Italian beef on everyone’s radar, and the rise of tavern-style pizza around the country.

The Midwest has always had great restaurants, of course, but it’s undeniable that something has shifted. “People are flying into these cities rather than flying over them,” says Vinnie Cimino, the Cleveland chef who co-owns Rosy and Cordelia. “I think that word is getting out about these smaller pockets of culture and cuisine.” Some of this is attributable to diners being more willing to explore outside big coastal cities, but it’s also due to chefs returning home to the region. “Post-pandemic, a lot of folks moved out of larger cities and back home,” says Cimino. “Now they’re setting up shop and creating great things in the spaces that they grew up in.” David Posey, chef and co-owner of Creepies and Elske in Chicago, agrees, adding: “For a long time, it felt like we were playing catch-up with trends on the coasts. Now I think we’re less quick to follow trends and are more confident in having our own voice of what the Midwest is.”

One of those chefs who left New York is Knall, a Birmingham, Alabama, native who cooked at Gramercy Tavern in New York before moving to his wife’s hometown of Milwaukee in 2020. Another is Peter Hoang, who worked at his father’s Kansas City, Missouri, sushi restaurant before gaining experience in Chicago and New York restaurants. When he returned to open Akoya Omakase, he crafted menus with the audience in mind, with two omakases, priced more affordably than many at $85 and $165, as well as an à la carte menu. “My sushi is honed by Japanese techniques and sourcing,” he says. “But I interpret what I think is best for the fish, whether that’s highlighting the textures and flavors through different garnishes or using aging or salting techniques.”

It’s not simply that these are good restaurants located in the Midwest—these restaurants are deeply Midwestern in ethos. In Chicago, David and Anna Posey, who run the Michelin-starred Elske, wanted to open a French bistro for their second venture. But as they developed Creepies with chef de cuisine Tayler Ploshehanski, David Posey says they began expanding its focus: “We started taking flavors and adapting them to things that we’re a little more familiar with.” This means dishes that draw on the traditions of Michigan, Wisconsin, and Illinois—think tarte flambée on a tavern-style pizza crust and mussels with giardiniera. And it’s not just the food at Creepies that reflects the Midwest: “We told our designer that our inspiration board was a Midwest basement with wood paneling and low ceilings meets a bistro in the French countryside.”

At Cordelia, Cimino leans into the traditional cuisine of Northeast Ohio, with offerings like raw-beef cannibal sandwiches and kielbasa with cabbage salad. “It’s the familiar flavors that we grew up eating, rethought into this more modern light,” he says. Meanwhile, Rosy “is a deeper dive into the culture of our region” and features dishes like Balkan cevapi and Italian cotechino cooked over live fire. The approach is drawing a wide range of Cleveland diners, from 20-somethings there for the cool, candlelit vibe to grandparents there to taste the food they grew up with. “I think that’s what the Midwest is,” Cimino says. “Being able to be that transgenerational space everybody feels welcome in.”

That welcoming community sensibility is a key component of Midwestern restaurants. Knall counts several farmers and shoppers at the West Allis Farmers Market, where he sources for Cassis, as some of his regulars. “To me, it shows that’s really what Midwest food is: supporting those communities,” he says.

Perhaps more than anything, it’s hospitality that sets these spots apart. “Hospitality is our biggest focus between both restaurants and maybe even more of a focus than the food,” Knall says. “To me, the way that our team makes you feel in the restaurants is such a Midwest thing.” And at Cordelia, where the slogan is “Midwest Nice,” Cimino says: “It’s welcoming you into our proverbial home.”

All the must-see supermoons, meteor showers, star clusters, constellations and deep sky objects this winter — and the gear you need to see them.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Winter is an incredible time for stargazing. With the long hours of darkness and an impressive variety of celestial objects on display, it's easy to fall in love with the night sky during the winter. Whether you have binoculars, a telescope, a smart telescope or are just observing with your eyes, there's something for everyone to enjoy over the coming months.

We've listed all the best sights to see this winter, including the supermoons, star clusters, galaxies and deep-sky nebulae that are best placed in the sky in December, January and February. We see the return of Orion and the Pleiades, with Jupiter and Saturn also making their way back into the night sky, while December also has one of the best and brightest meteor showers of the entire year — the Geminids.

This is by no means an exhaustive list of everything you can see — we'd be here until July — but just a collection of some of our favorite winter sights. Some, like the supermoons and planets, are specific to 2026/2027 timings, but the constellations and deep sky objects we see over the winter are something stargazers look forward to all year. Something to get us through the cold, dreary weather, and a reassuring sign that we made it through another year.

A composite photo of a full supermoon rising into the sky.

This winter is host to three consecutive supermoons (in addition to the full Beaver Supermoon on Nov. 24, making four in a row). The first, and the most festive, is the Christmas Eve supermoon, peaking on December 24, 2026, at 01:28 UTC (which works out as late evening on the 23rd in North America). This last moon of the year is traditionally called the Cold Moon, and this supermoon will look up to 14% larger and 30% brighter than a normal full moon.

The first full moon of 2027, known as the Wolf Moon, peaks on January 22, 2027 at 12:17 UTC. Finally, the super Snow Moon peaks on February 20, 2027 at 23:24 UTC, coinciding with a penumbral lunar eclipse. This is when the sun, moon and Earth line up loosely during a full moon, causing the moon to pass through the Earth's faint outer shadow — the penumbra. During this type of eclipse, the moon only dims slightly, so it won't be nearly as dramatic as a blood moon eclipse.

A photo of an annular, or "ring of fire", solar eclipse.

Observers in South America and Africa will witness an annular solar eclipse on February 6, 2027, peaking at around 16:00 UTC. It will appear as a "ring of fire" in the sky, as an annular solar eclipse happens when the moon passes between Earth and the sun when the moon is near or at its farthest from Earth, known as apogee. Unlike a total solar eclipse, the sun isn't totally blocked, and the sky doesn't turn dark.

A photo of a bright planet glowing in the evening sky.

Since Saturn made its return to the evening sky in the fall, it rises earlier and earlier over the winter months, making this a great time to observe Saturn at a reasonable hour. There are still a few years before we will see the rings at full tilt again, but in 2026/2027 we can start to see more details in the rings after the planet appeared edge-on last year.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

To get a good glimpse of Saturn this winter, you'll need a telescope with at least 4 or 5 inches of aperture and a good eyepiece that gives you at least 100x magnification. Smart telescopes and binoculars don't have the reach, so this is a job for an observational telescope. But that's all right; the hill we'll die on is that there's nothing that'll take your breath away quite like seeing Saturn's rings with your own eyes.

Jupiter will reach opposition on the night of February 10-11, 2027, when it will be at its brightest and closest to Earth, making it appear its largest in the sky. This is the perfect time to observe it with your telescope to see the bands and the Great Red Spot, as well as its four Galilean moons. You'll be able to see the moons with a pair of big astronomy binoculars (we can see them with our 15x70’s), but you'll need a telescope to make out any of the finer details on the planet itself.

After almost a year of absence, Mars made its return to the evening sky in November (albeit quite late in the evening) and will reach opposition on February 19, 2027. Despite being one of our closest neighboring planets, Mars is notoriously difficult to get any meaningful observations with via a telescope, so its opposition is the best chance you'll have.

You'd be forgiven for thinking that because Mars is technically closer to Earth than Jupiter, Saturn and deep-sky objects like the Andromeda Galaxy or the Orion Nebula, viewing it through a telescope would be a breeze, but that's not the case. Mars is very small, with low-contrast features, and only comes observably close to Earth for a few months at a time around every 26-27 months, so it demands quite a lot from a telescope. Even with larger telescopes, it'll only show up as a fuzzy orange dot most of the time.

If you want to try viewing Mars with a telescope this opposition, you'll need 4-6 inches of aperture minimum, depending on what kind of telescope you have. However, for Mars, it's arguably more important to have good seeing (unfortunate with the nearly full moon on this day), excellent quality optics, a stable (preferably motorized) mount, a good focuser and an eyepiece with good eye relief that gives 100x magnification or more to observe any of the planet's finer details.

Alternatively, if you're more of a beginner and are just starting your stargazing hobby, you can head outside with just your eyes and go "Hey look, there's Mars. Cool!" and be done with it.

The Geminids meteor shower is active from December 4-20, peaking on the night of December 13-14, 2026. The waxing crescent moon sets early, leaving dark skies after around 9 pm for prime meteor viewing, and this is one of the few meteor showers that very kindly peaks before midnight.

The Geminids are one of the strongest meteor showers of the year, and this year’s show is expected to have around 120 to 150 meteors per hour under clear, dark skies — making it an exciting opportunity for astrophotography.

Unlike most meteor showers, which come from icy comets, the Geminids originate from a rocky asteroid called 3200 Phaethon. The debris from this asteroid is much denser than the dust from comets, making it able to survive deeper into the atmosphere before burning up. This results in brighter, stronger and more colorful fireballs than the other meteor showers.

If the Geminids left you hooked on meteor showers, you'll only have a few weeks to wait until the Ursids peak on December 22-23, 2026.

However, there are a couple of hurdles here. First, the activity rate is usually quite low — between 5 and 10 meteors per hour. Second, the nearly full moon will hinder visibility and limit sightings to only the brightest meteors. However, as they originate from Ursa Minor, which is circumpolar, the peak viewing time of 21:00-22:00 UTC is much friendlier than the showers that peak in the middle of the night, so it won't require an unreasonable amount of commitment if you do want to catch them.

The first meteor shower of 2027, the Quadrantids, is active between December 28, 2026 and January 28, 2027, peaking on the night of January 3-4, 2027. The thin waning crescent moon won't interfere with viewing conditions, and we could see up to 100-120 meteors per hour. The best time to view will be from midnight through to the pre-dawn hours, when the radiant point, Bootes, is highest in the sky.

Canis Major (the "Greater Dog") is visible over the winter months through until spring, and is easily recognisable by Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky. It's one of the closest stars to our solar system, sitting 8.6 light-years away, and due to its distance and apparent magnitude, its twinkling and flashes of color are particularly noticeable. This is known as scintillation, where turbulence in Earth's atmosphere bends starlight as it passes through different layers of air. It's especially noticeable when Sirius is low in the sky, as the light has more atmosphere to pass through.

You don't need any specialist gear to spot Sirius — it's easily visible with the naked eye. However, if you do have a pair of binoculars, you can even try to spot it in the daytime at certain times of the year.

Look above Canis Major, and you'll find Canis Minor — the "Little Dog". It primarily consists of two bright stars: Procyon and Gomeisa, the former making up a key part of the Winter Triangle and Winter Hexagon. Canis Minor is a fairly faint constellation, but a pair of binoculars will give you a better view.

Canis Minor and Canis Major are most famously known as the loyal hunting dogs of Orion, who spent seven years pursuing the Pleiades sisters to no avail. He should have just led with the fact that he had two dogs.

Speaking of Orion, one of the most recognizable sights in the night sky is Orion's belt, consisting of three bright stars in a straight line: Alnitak, Alnilam and Mintaka. Because of its prominence in the winter sky, Orion's belt has served as a universal celestial marker for navigation, timekeeping and mythologies across human history. The entire Orion constellation is a favorite among stargazers because there's so much to see, both with the naked eye and through binoculars or a telescope.

Another prominent feature of the Orion constellation is Betelgeuse. This red supergiant is easily visible to the naked eye, and astronomers expect it to explode as a supernova within the next 100,000 years. When that eventually happens, it will become visible in broad daylight and shine as brightly as the full moon for a few months. Betelgeuse, Sirius (Canis Major) and Procyon (Canis Minor) make up the Winter Triangle.

There's also Rigel, the brightest star in the constellation, which marks the hunter's foot, and Orion's Sword, a hanging line of stars just below the belt, which contains the Orion Nebula (more on that later).

Although Taurus returned to the evening sky in the fall, winter offers the best viewing time because it sits higher earlier in the evening. The brightest star in the constellation, Aldebaran, is easily recognizable as an orange-red star that marks the bull's eye.

With a pair of binoculars, you'll be able to see two beautiful star clusters — the Pleiades (M45) and the Hyades. The former is a bright open star cluster consisting of seven stars (also known as the Seven Sisters) that you can just about see with the naked eye under very dark skies, and the latter is a V-shaped open cluster that forms the face and head of the bull.

The Pleiades is an ideal first target if you're thinking of buying an entry-level smart telescope, and it's also easy to pick out in wide-field iPhone photos of the night sky.

Auriga is a pentagon-shaped constellation high in the sky between Taurus and Gemini, and is home to a few star clusters to observe this winter.

M36, the Pinwheel Cluster, contains around 60 to 100 stars and is located north of the star El Nath in Auriga. M38, known as the Starfish Cluster, contains over 100 stars, with its brightest forming an X shape, giving it a starfish-like appearance. Finally, M37, known as the Salt and Pepper Cluster, is the brightest and richest cluster in the constellation and contains over 500 stars.

Not only is Gemini the radiant point of the Geminids meteor shower, but its two most prominent stars, Pollux and Castor, are a very recognizable winter target in the night sky. Pollux is an orange giant star and the constellation's brightest point, while Castor appears blue. Although Castor looks like one star to the naked eye, it's actually a complex multiple star system, consisting of three distinct binary pairs: Castor A, Castor B and Castor C. With a small telescope, you can split Castor into its two main pairs, Castor Aa and Castor Ba.

Gemini also contains M35, a large open cluster also known as the Shoe Buckle Cluster, which you can easily view with binoculars.

It’s not an official constellation, but the Winter Hexagon (also known as the Winter Circle) is a recognizable pattern of prominent stars in the winter sky. It consists of Rigel (Orion), Aldebaran (Taurus), Capella (Auriga), Pollux (Gemini), Procyon (Canis Minor) and Sirius (Canis Major).

Once you spot all of the stars that make up the Winter Hexagon, it provides an easy way to navigate your way around the night sky with your binoculars or telescope.

Probably everyone's favorite nebula, largely because it's very easy to spot. It's located in Orion's sword, just below Orion's belt, and when conditions are dark enough, you can even see it with the naked eye and identify it in smartphone photos. Binoculars reveal it as a faint smudge, while telescopes give you a better view of the bright, glowing gas. It's also a wonderful target for smart telescopes with a wide field of view.

While you're there, you can find the Running Man Nebula, a bright reflection nebula complex located just north of the Orion Nebula — and it can be captured in the same frame if you're photographing it. If nebulas are your thing, Orion is absolutely packed with them, including the Casper the Friendly Ghost Nebula (M78), the Monkey Head Nebula (NGC 2174) and the Witch Head Nebula (IC 2118), although many of Orion's nebulas are quite faint and tricky to capture, requiring long integration times.

A photo of the Horsehead and Flame Nebulas

The Horsehead and Flame Nebula in Orion is another popular target for smart telescopes, as it takes up a big portion of the frame and doesn't need a super-long integration time to get a decent, web-ready image (although we'd always recommend shooting for as long as you can).

The Flame and Horsehead are technically two separate entities, but are often paired together due to their close apparent proximity, often fitting inside the same frame. The Flame Nebula is a bright, vibrant emission nebula that gets its name from its fiery network of dark, dense dust lanes. The Horsehead Nebula, on the other hand, is a dark nebula. It's composed of a dense cloud of molecular dust and gas that blocks the light from the emission nebula and stars around it. As the name suggests, this dark nebula takes on the form of a horse's head and neck.

The Rosette Nebula is a vast, star-forming region in the constellation of Monoceros and is a fantastic astrophotography target. Its large, flower-like appearance comes from stellar winds and radiation from the central cluster of young stars. The best time to view and photograph the Rosette Nebula is from January, when Monoceros climbs higher and higher in the evening sky.

The California Nebula lives in the constellation Perseus and gets its name from its resemblance to the U.S. state. This famous emission nebula is made up of ionized gas from the nearby Xi Persei, giving it its vibrant red and pink appearance. It has an apparent size of approximately 2.5 degrees, making it a great target for astrophotography and smart telescopes, as it appears quite large in the frame. Peak visibility of the California Nebula is from now until February.

12,000 light-years away, in the constellation Auriga, you'll find the Tadpole Nebula — a beautiful emission nebula and active stellar nursery. It spans 100 light-years across and makes for a stunning smart telescope target. It gets its name from the distinct, prominent gas and dust pillars that resemble cosmic tadpoles swimming through space — only these tadpoles are around 10 light-years long.

If you're using a smart telescope or astrophotography camera, you'll typically need an integration time of 2-3 hours to bring out more structure in the nebulosity, although longer sessions will yield better results.

Also in Auriga is the Flaming Star Nebula, although this nebula is much closer to Earth — around 1,500 light-years away — and spans about 5 light-years across. Despite being "smaller" than other targets, it appears quite big in the frame of a smart telescope due to its distance from Earth. It's best seen throughout late autumn and winter when Auriga is climbing high in the sky.

The Flaming Star Nebula is an emission and reflection nebula, with each type of nebulosity responding to different filters. In this instance, capturing two sets of data to stack in astrophotography software can help reveal more detail and colors. Broadband filter exposures capture the full range of visible light, including the blue light reflected by dust, as well as natural star colors. Narrowband or dual-band filters isolate specific emission wavelengths, such as hydrogen-alpha (Ha) and oxygen-III (OIII). By using these filters for separate sessions, your final image will show the red glow from the emission nebula and the blue tones from the reflective dust.

Kimberley Lane, E-commerce writer for Live Science, has tested a wide range of optical equipment, reviewing camera gear from Sony, Canon, OM System and more. With over 6 years of photography experience, her skills span across landscape and seascape photography, wildlife, astrophotography and portrait work. Her photos have been featured in a number of national magazines, including Digital Camera World and Cosmopolitan. She has also contributed to our sister site Space.com and Tech Radar, and she regularly uses binoculars and telescopes to stargaze in the dark skies of South Wales.

#6380. ALMA Reveals a Dying Star's Final Breath, Encoded In a Giant Ring of Gas

Stars transition through different stages as they evolve. Sun-like stars with low to intermediate masses (about 0.8 to 8 solar masses) begin as main-sequence stars, then transition sequentially to red giants, asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars, then post-AGB stars. By the end, they leave behind only a planetary nebula. Each of those transitions are detailed and complicated, and astrophysicists crave a more complete understanding of them.

Stars in their AGB phase have an important job. They spread heavy elements into the surrounding interstellar medium (ISM) and those elements are taken up in subsequent star and planet formation. As they transition from AGB phase to post-AGB phase, they experience thermal pulses that expel material. These events are like brief snapshots in the long life of a star, and catching one in the act is challenging.

Astronomers working with the Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA) have caught a star after what seems to be its final thermal pulse, leaving behing a planetary nebula. This is a rare opportunity to study this transition in detail.

âWeâve caught, for the first time, a starâs final nuclear heartbeat, frozen in gas.â - Raghvendra Sahai, NASA/JPL.

Their observations are in new research titled "The Last Gasps of a Dying Star: ALMA Observations of the Preplanetary Nebula IRAS 06530â0213." It's published in The Astrophysical Journal, and the lead author is Raghvendra Sahai, senior research scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

IRAS 06530â0213 is a preplanetary nebula (PPN) about 12,000 light years away. Astronomers have been watching it for years as it takes shape. They know that the preplanetary nebula phase is a critical evolutionary stage in a star's transition from the asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stage to the planetary nebula (PN) stage. PPN structures contain critical insights that aren't available in any other way.

"These data show the presence of an extended circular ringâfirst evidence of the last thermal pulse preceding the post-asymptotic giant branch (AGB) phase in a carbon starâand a central bipolar nebula (CBN) and torus," the authors write. The outer ring came from the last thermal pulse about 6500 years ago, and is the first direct evidence of this type of thermal pulse that's emitted before a star like this begins its final phase.

This snapshot is all about the mass-loss stars experience as they die, and the authors explain that the AGB progenitor's mass-loss rate "decreased immediately after the thermal pulse, then rose again just before the post-AGB phase."

The mass-loss dropped off for about 2,000 years, then for about 1,000 years after that, it rose again. The filamentary structures around around the CBN are evidence of the star emitting a thick and lumpy shell of gas. An hourglass-shaped nebula with a torus is inside the filamentary arc region.

This ALMA image of IRAS 06530 show the PPN's structure. The outer molecular ring is from its progenitor star's final thermal pulse. The CBN is the central bipolar nebula, and the FAR is the filamentary arc region. The FAR is evidence of the progenitor's mass loss rate dropping immediately after the thermal pulse, then rising again just before the star's post-AGB phase. Image Credit: ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO); Sahai et al. (2026)

Based on the expansion ages of the torus and the CBN, Sahai and his co-researchers determined that the progenitor star transitioned to a post-AGB star around only 700 yrs ago, maybe a little less than that. That is a remarkably short amount of time to have lapsed since its transition, considering stellar ages.

In 2003 it was first identified as a carbon-rich PPN, and its envelope expansion velocity was measured. Subsequent research identified its s-process enrichment, where elements heavier than iron are synthesized. Then in 2025, this paper identified the PPN's spherical halo and central barrel-shaped torus.

Luck might not describe these most recent observations, because those prior observations were the primer, but good fortune might. The kind of good fortune that finds its way to people who spend their lives watching stars.

âMost of us think of stars as unchanging points of light, but this is a real-time snapshot of a starâs death throes,â said lead author Sahai, author and co-author of more than 140 published papers. âItâs the brief, violent transition between a bloated red giant and a glowing planetary nebula, frozen mid-action.â

There is something puzzling in this PPN and its filamentary arc region that still needs an explanation. "The arc stuctures are likely part of a 3D Archimedean spiral structure generally attributed to the presence of a binary companion," the authors write.

This image shows the central region of IRAS 06530, showing filamentary arc structures with dashed green, cyan, and white arcs. These arcs are typical signatures of a binary companion, but the researchers didn't fine one. Image Credit: ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO); Sahai et al. (2026)

Dying stars with companions not only have spiral structures, but they're normally found inside compact dust disks. The disks are evidence of mass-transfer with a close binary companion. The mass-transfer is usually the cause of the hourglass-shapes. But the researchers didn't find a dusty disk, the usual signature of a companion.

"However, we do not find a compact continuum source at the location of IRAS 06530âs central star, such as that associated with the compact dusty disks typically found in disk-prominent post-AGB objects known to have binary companions," the researchers explain.

âDying stars so often have hidden companions that reshape their ejected material into intricate, bipolar or multipolar forms instead of simple spheres,â said Sahai. âIRAS 06530 shows that the story is more complicated than the tidy explanation weâve been using.â

IRAS 06530 also has a chemical composition that's challenging to understand. It's significantly enriched in 13C, 17O, and modestly enriched in 15N.

"Compared with solar values, the torus of IRAS 06530 appears to be significantly (modestly) enriched in 13C and 17O (15N), as wellâa pattern of rare-isotope enrichment inconsistent with standard nucleosynthesis models," the authors write.

Â¹Â³C and Â¹â·O are expected, but Â¹âµN isn't. It should be destroyed and depleted to solar levels. Again, a binary companion could be one explanation for this anomaly, and future observations might find one. It's also possible that atypical bursts of nuclear burning are responsible, but that's beyond the scope of this work.

Finding the first direct evidence of a dying star's thermal pulse, something indicated by theory, is the kind of progress astrophysicists hope to make.

âItâs essentially a physical snapshot of an event that, until now, weâve mostly inferred from theoretical models,â said Sahai. âWeâve caught, for the first time, a starâs final nuclear heartbeat, frozen in gas.â

#6378. The Physics Wall Facing Orbital AI Data Centers

Basing entire business plans on back-of-the-envelope calculations might not seem like the best idea. However, according to a new paper available in preprint on arXiv by Dr. Slava Turyshev of NASAâs Jet Propulsion Laboratory, that is precisely what the companies touting orbital AI data centers are doing. While on paper, the math looks good, the physical constraints of actually utilizing all the processing power and free energy of the Sun that orbit provides is prohibitive in a number of ways - and it will be a long time before we have the technology to truly capitalize on the advantages of space-based AI.

First, letâs dig into what the back-of-the-envelope calculations say. Research from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory suggests that U.S.-based data centers could consume 580 terawatt-hours of electricity over a five-year window, an increase of around 17-46 gigawatts compared to modern levels. But land-based data centers are running into plenty of bottlenecks, from newly elected hostile politicians to hard caps on the electrical gridâs ability to supply all that additional power.

So the solution seems obvious - launch the data centers into orbit, where they will be beyond any individual NIMBY protesters, have access to essentially unlimited free solar power, and not have to deal with water cooling systems. Sounds pretty good. Until the actual physics of what that means comes into play.

Fraser addresses the idea of data centers in space.

There are three main physics hurdles that all culminate into a giant economic one facing data centers, and it all comes down to scale. Size and weight are the first major obstacle. Dr. Turyshev uses a baseline 1-megawatt orbital processing facility as an example. It would hold roughly the processing power of a small commercial server room. But in space it would require 5,640 square meters of deployed solar panels, even in a âdawn-duskâ orbit designed to minimize the time it spends in Earthâs shadow. Thatâs roughly the size of an American football field.

On top of that, the spacecraft would need around 2,500 square meters of radiator panels to stop the electronics from frying themselves. Combining the power generation and cooling equipment required would already bring a spacecraft up to 30 metric tons. Adding in structural trusses, control thrusters, and radiation shielding brings the total mass of 1 MW of orbital data capacity is likely between 34 and 59 metric tons.

For the purposes of practicality, Dr. Turyshev then drops down to a 100 kW center, since a 1 MW data center would not even fit in many modern rocket fairings. Arguably, since each 100 kW data center wouldnât be exactly 10% of the weight of a 1 MW data center, he uses a rough estimate of around 5 metric tons for a single spacecraft of that size. The problem is, to keep up with demand, we would need to launch between 170,000 and 461,000 of them over the course of five years. And each Falcon 9 can only launch at most four of them. That would require almost 9,000 Falcon 9 launches over the next five years - or roughly 33 of them per week.

Fraser talks about turning the Moon into a data center.

Even if we had the launch capacity for that sheer scale, there is another bottleneck to contend with - getting the data back to Earth. As we reported earlier this week, weâve made great strides in high-speed optical communications down from orbit lately. However, the headline number of 200 gigabits per second is a single point in time. These âhigh speedâ links realistically deliver around 13 to 26 gigabits per second continuously, in part because they require a direct line of sight to the ground station theyâre communicating with, and they also canât communicate through clouds. Even if we flooded major parts of the Earthâs surface with ground stations, those speeds would severely hobble any interactive cloud apps or data-heavy training runs that require continual syncing with anything on the ground.

But even if we solved the communications problem, thereâs still the problem of that omnipresent menace in space - radiation. Cosmic rays are famous for flipping single bits in computer memory, constantly forcing processors to run error-checking algorithms, and thereby eating into usable computer time. According to the paper, over a five-year mission, the cumulative radiation damage and micrometeoroid impacts would continually degrade both the electronics and solar panels, driving up the cost of every calculation completed.

With all that in mind, the economic hurdle becomes very clear. On Earth, a high-end AI data center costs between $10,000 and $40,000 per kilowatt of computing capacity. In order for a 40-kilogram per kilowatt orbital satellite to match that pricing, it would need combined launch and manufacturing costs of between $250 and $1,000 per kilogram. For comparison, current dedicated Falcon 9 launches work out to roughly $3,360 per kilogram. So the launch cost alone is three to thirteen times more expensive than the entire combined launch and manufacturing cost of a single data center.

Video from Astraveo arguing the same physics as what Dr. Turyshev talks about in the paper. Credit - Astraveo YouTube Channel

With all that said, there are some niche applications for orbital computing in the near future, according to the paper. The first is space-native processing, where satellites crunch the raw imagery for Earth-observation satellites or sensor data before broadcasting high-value insights back down to Earth. Another is communications-based edge computing, where processors piggyback on existing constellations like Starlink that already pay for solar arrays, lasers, and ground stations.

But ultimately, despite this paper, various organizations are moving forward with their plans for data centers in orbit. Even today (November 25th) the FCC approved SpaceXâs application to launch one million âStarmindâ orbital data centers by 2040. Earlier this month, Google booked a flight on a Blue Origin rocket for a test of its Project Suncatcher computing constellation. Until the real economics of the situation catch up with them, it might be a while before these efforts realize what hard physical limits theyâre going up against.

S. G. Turyshev - Orbital Data Centers: Spacecraft Constraints and Economic Viability
