#6333. The 6 Best Portable Generators Give You Power Whenever and Wherever You Need It

These editor-tested models are ideal for camping, tailgating, or powering tools when you’re too far from an outlet.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Generators come in all sizes, but when you need power for camping or tailgating, or to power tools when you’re too far from an outlet, a large one meant for home backup is just too much. Power stations are handy, but once they run out of power, they take a long time to recharge. That’s where a smaller-sized portable generator can really shine. So long as you have the fuel, they can keep running.

When you’re shopping for a portable generator, there are a few important things to consider, including power, weight, and fuel type. For portable power, models that output 2,000 to 5,000 watts will generally be simple enough to lift in and out of a truck, though some models that generate more are designed to be lightweight. Anything over 100 pounds starts to buck the idea of something being portable, even if it has wheels.

Fuel type matters, too. All generators run on gas, but dual-fuel models can also run on propane. The drawback is that propane delivers slightly less power output and shorter running time, but it runs a lot cleaner and is much less messy to deal with.

If you’re powering sensitive electronics like digital equipment or TVs, you’ll also want to look for an inverter generator, which delivers more stable “cleaner” power that won’t damage your gear. They also run quieter than standard models. For these reasons, all of the picks on our list are inverter generators.

Keeping portability in mind, the models we cover in this story are all 7,500 watts and under. For the models that we tested, we based our methods on our experience using generators for backup power with and without transfer switches, on construction sites to run power tools and equipment, as well as running sound systems and lighting at outdoor events. We measured the sound levels of these generators idling with no load, and while running under load at two feet and 25 feet. We then used an oscilloscope to observe the sine wave of the alternating current generated by these machines, and a clamp meter to check voltage output.

Some examples of devices we used with large starting and running loads include a large air conditioner and a portable table saw. In one case, we even tested it paired to a solar inverter-charger. We evaluated these generators based on ease of starting, power response, sound levels, value, safety, and reliability to select the top performers.

The Honda EU2200i inverter generator has just about everything you want from a portable generator. It’s half the size and weight of comparable generators in its class; it’s very quiet and clean when operating; and it’s fully enclosed so you can quickly and easily transport it and move it around without worrying about it getting caught on anything.

That enclosure is an important feature, as it protects the inverter electronics and helps contain noise—the EU2200i is remarkably quiet. In testing, we measured sound levels of 68.9 decibels at the generator under no load. When we switched it to “eco” mode, which reduces engine speed when power isn’t called for, the sound was reduced to 76 decibels.

When we used an oscilloscope to look at the sine wave of the current generated, the curves were smooth and symmetrical, an indicator of “clean” power. This remained true even when running heavy loads from devices like a table saw or an air conditioner.

There are some nice design features, too. The vent on the gas cap closes so fumes or fuel cannot escape. You could breathe freely packing this in the passenger compartment of an SUV. Likewise, the power on/off switch doubles as a fuel shutoff, so it can’t be forgotten.

Lastly, the EU2200i has ports for parallel operation. With the correct cable kit, it connects to a second EU2200i to double the output to 4,400 starting and 3,600 running watts. The EU2200i is ideal for camping and other outdoor events where generator noise might be frowned on.

We like the GD400BN because it’s powerful, quiet, and portable at a reasonable price point. The interesting thing about this inverter generator is how much power it can deliver, yet it’s still as compact as similar generators that deliver half as much output. Even when running on lower-output propane as the fuel source, it can run up to 3,000 watts, which is considerable for a generator that only weighs 47 pounds.

Another plug or two would’ve been nice, however. Its single AC outlet limits you to plugging one power tool or appliance at a time, despite having enough output to power more than one device. It does have a 120-volt, 30-amp outlet for connecting to an RV, though, so that does make up for it a bit, but only if you have that need. The 1.1-gallon fuel tank is also a bit limiting regarding runtime for gasoline, but that’s easily overcome by using propane. For all intents and purposes, this is a very nice dual-fuel generator, and at a list price of $600, it comes at a reasonable price to boot.

The Wen DF360iX offers a considerable amount of utility for an affordable price. You have the option to run the generator on gasoline or propane with a running output of up to 2,900 watts. While propane delivers a bit less at 2,600 watts, that’s plenty of power for a job site or camping use and even enough electricity for small to midsize RVs.

While this generator is fairly light at 49 pounds, it doesn’t cut back on ports, including a 30-amp port for direct connection to an RV. There are also two three-prong AC ports, a 12-volt DC receptacle, and two USB-A ports. Like most inverter generators, it produces less noise. This model is rated at around 65 decibels of noise at a quarter load, which is quiet enough that it shouldn’t bother the neighbors. There are some nice safety features, too, including auto-shutoff if the fuel runs too low and a carbon monoxide (CO) sensor that detects if dangerous levels are present.

Of course, with any generator in this price range (under $500), there are compromises. This model has a pretty small fuel tank—only 1.5 gallons—so you won’t be able to run this on gasoline for long periods (around five hours with a half-load) without having to stop and refill. You can mitigate this, however, by relying on a larger tank of propane. For example, a 20-pound tank should enable you to run it for up to 14 hours.

GENERATOR SAFETYWhile not hard to run, generators present dangers, so you need to follow basic safety rules. Never operate them in a closed space, like a garage or shed. Exhaust gases contain carbon monoxide (CO), a lethal, odorless, colorless gas. Most manufacturers offer models that shut down when they detect carbon monoxide building up. Do not run a generator in a garage with the door open, or in front of the garage with the door open, because carbon monoxide can still get trapped and seep into the house. Run generators at least 20 feet away, including from windows and doors, with the exhaust blowing away from the house.

RV owners need a generator outfitted with at least a 120-volt, 30-amp outlet, but it also helps to have a decent amount of power to go with it, so that you can run things like a heater or an air conditioner. This model from Champion offers both, with the outlet and up to 3,500 running watts, which is enough to power a small- to medium-sized RV.

It also offers great fuel flexibility. With a full 2.3-gallon fuel tank, it should be able to run for up to 14 hours, but it’s dual-fuel, so with a full 20-pound propane tank, this generator can supply 21 hours of uninterrupted power.

In addition to being a solid companion for camping and RVing, this generator could serve as a useful tool in an emergency at home where power is needed. Using a manual transfer switch, you could power a few 120-volt circuits using the 30-amp connection. And the inverter will help to keep it running more quietly, which is helpful at home or the campground.

One of our test editors picked up this generator when faced with a home emergency where he needed a generator with specific features, quickly, and on a budget. A failed generator at a solar-powered off-grid cabin necessitated the quick acquisition, and, happily, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel Inverter Generator showed up on the doorstep in only two days.

In about 15 minutes, with minimal assembly and after adding oil, the generator was connected to a propane cylinder by a hose and was running on the first cycle of the starter. Since then, it’s run steadily at 500 watts, up to 5,500 watts, at 240 volts (great for powering high-voltage appliances like dryers or water pumps), to charge a battery bank during the winter when sunlight wasn’t enough to get the job done.

This Pulsar puts out very clean power, too, with a claimed total harmonic distortion (THD) of less than 3 percent, which met the requirements of the solar inverter-charger it was paired with.

Using the inverter to monitor the current frequency, we found that it was indeed very stable with minimal variance, between 59.97 and 60.09 Hz. All things considered, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel is a good value for the specs, capacity, and features.

Generac’s iQ3800 Portable Inverter Generator is a great example of what we love about dual-fuel, inverter generators. This type of generator can deliver cleaner power than a standard model, meaning there’s less distortion in the electrical current frequency. That’s ideal for powering sensitive electronics, such as TVs, computer equipment, and smart household appliances. This is also a closed-frame inverter generator, which tends to be quieter; the iQ3800 is one of the quietest generators we’ve tested of this size.

We were very impressed with how easy the iQ3800 is to operate. The electric start and auto choke worked perfectly, taking only about four to five seconds, while the manual pull-start also fired up the generator with minimal effort. Switching between fuel types was also very simple to perform. Once running, you can view important information on an easy-to-read LED display that lists the total hours the machine has run, the fuel level for the gasoline tank (there’s no gauge for propane), and a load gauge that uses a bar graph to show power output level—knowing that helps to avoid overloading the generator.

The inverter technology might be the most important feature of the iQ3800. This generator has a total harmonic distortion (THD)—a level of variance in the current frequency—of less than 3 percent, which is very low. Essentially, anything with a screen or any smart device would be best powered using an inverter generator like the iQ3800. It’s an ideal generator to power RVs in campgrounds or off-grid, and a great option for emergency backup in urban areas.

Full Generac iQ3800 Portable Inverter Generator Review

These generators, sometimes called backup generators, are used to provide temporary power when and where it is needed. Portable is a relative term; some are more portable than others. While the smallest models can be picked up and carried, most have wheels and a handle to make transport easier. However, at 100 pounds or more, picking them up to load or move may take two people. Appliances, power tools, or other devices can be plugged directly into standard outlets on the generator’s front panel.

Additionally, many models have a twist-lock plug that can provide up to 240 volts and be used to power circuits in a home via a manual transfer switch. You may hear generators like these referred to as “open frame” generators, which simply means that the engine, fuel tank, and generator components are not enclosed in bodywork.

Though inverter-type generators are—like their standard cousins—typically portable, we group them separately because they’re significantly and technically different in terms of how they work.

Like most generators, inverter generators provide 120/240 volts of AC power. They generate AC current just like the others, but it’s then converted to DC (Direct Current), and then inverted back to AC. The conversion and inversion is controlled by circuitry which acts like a filter, flattens surges, and cleans up the sine wave (or oscillating wave) of the electrical current.

Typical generators have varying degrees of distortion in the sine wave of the alternating current. This isn’t usually an issue for most electrical devices, though sensitive electronics like tablets, laptops, televisions, and other smart devices can be damaged by current distortion or surges. These devices will last longer with “clean” power and steady voltage. Because of that added complication, inverter generators can be significantly more expensive.

Standby generators are permanently installed and connected to a home. These may power selected, critical circuits during a power outage, or may provide power for the whole home. Standby generators have systems that monitor power supplied by a utility and start automatically in the event of an outage. Since they’re not portable or easily moved, we didn’t include any here.

It’s important to know what you intend to power with a generator in order to choose the right size. Manufacturers list two figures for generators: starting watts and running watts. Starting watts include the initial surge required to start appliances or tools with powerful electric motors or compressors. Once started, these devices require far less power to run continuously.

Many manufacturers have a chart with estimated power requirements for common appliances and tools to help you figure out what you need. For a more precise measurement, you can also calculate the figure yourself by adding up the power consumption of specific appliances and adding them together.

To calculate watts, multiply voltage (usually 120 volts) by the amps (amperage) required to run the appliance (usually found on a tag attached to the appliance). Do this for each item that the generator will power.

Most portable generators are powered by gasoline, the most commonly available fuel. However, when using generators for emergency power, their infrequent use presents some issues to consider.

The first is that when big, catastrophic storms hit and power outages last for days, gas stations may struggle to meet demand, resulting in long lines. The second issue has to do with the infrequent use of backup generators, which may sit for months to years between uses.

Gasoline sitting in a carburetor will slowly evaporate over time, leaving gummy deposits that can block fuel from getting through, making it difficult or even impossible to start your generator without servicing. You can avoid this by closing the fuel valve and letting the generator run until it stalls, using up the remaining fuel in the carburetor. Also, over time, gasoline can oxidize or become “stale,” losing combustibility. It may also absorb water, which can then corrode fuel tanks and other metal components in the fuel system. Starting a generator regularly, as well as treating fuel with a stabilizer, can help fight these issues.

Ethanol-free gasoline, available at some gas stations, is also less susceptible to degradation over time than standard 87-octane pump gas; however, it’s still a good idea to mix the fuel going into your generator with stabilizer.

Dual-fuel generators can run on gasoline or liquified petroleum gas (LPG), commonly known as propane. Switching between the fuels is simple, and you won’t be tied to the availability of one type of fuel.

A big advantage of propane is that it’s very stable when stored for long periods of time. It won’t go stale, and it won’t gum up carburetors from sitting. Plus, some homes that use propane for other purposes may already have large storage tanks on the premises, foregoing the need to make repeated trips out for fuel.

The downside to propane is that it creates fewer BTUs (British Thermal Units, a measurement of energy) than the same amount of gasoline. So, a generator running on propane will have slightly reduced starting and running watts. On the plus side, though, it will also run a little quieter than those that run on gasoline.

While not as common, tri-fuel generators add an option to connect by natural gas. Some propane-powered generators can be converted to run on natural gas, as well. Like propane, natural gas can run cleaner and a little quieter. However, it also creates fewer BTUs than gasoline and propane, so it will also produce reduced starting and running watts.

Natural gas also requires a dedicated line for the generator, which most homes that have access to natural gas will not have, and thus will need to be professionally installed.

If you’re powering appliances, tools, or other devices by plugging them directly into the standard outlets on the generator, the answer is no. If the generator is being used to power circuits in your home, maybe. It’s always best to consult the operator’s manual, a licensed electrician, or your local building officials about township ordinances—some localities may have requirements that differ from the National Electrical Code (NEC).

Electrical circuits need to be grounded to operate devices safely, so that any current that shorts out or has a fault is directed to the ground, i.e., the actual, literal earth, so the user doesn’t become the conduit to “ground.”

There are two ways that generators are grounded: neutral-bonded and floating neutral. Neutral-bonded means the neutral wire is connected (i.e., bonded) to the generator frame. With a floating neutral, the neutral is not connected to the frame. In the latter case, the generator should be grounded by connecting the ground terminal to a grounding rod driven into the ground.

Generators with ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) outlets, when used to power circuits in your home, require neutral switching and a manual transfer switch, and must be grounded by connecting the ground terminal to a ground rod driven into the soil. Neutral-switching transfer switches are also referred to as three-pole transfer switches.

There could be numerous reasons for difficulty starting a generator. The first things to check are whether or not there's any fuel in the tank, and if the fuel valve is turned open. Then, check for any obstructions in the air cleaner box. If that’s clean, move on to check that the engine has spark.

If your generator has sat for a long time without treated fuel, the carburetor may be clogged up and require cleaning—if you’re unfamiliar with any of these steps, it may be best to take it to a shop for service.

In an emergency, use what you can get, but as a general rule, 87 octane fuel will be fine—just don’t go lower than that.

As long as we’re talking fuel, it’s always best to use ethanol-free fuel in equipment with small gas engines—if that’s not possible, nothing more than 10-percent ethanol. Ethanol can attract moisture, which will then separate and settle in the gas tank or carburetor, where it can corrode and clog the fuel system. For this reason, it’s also a good idea to treat gas with a fuel stabilizer.

Much like your lawn mower, generators need regular maintenance. However, since they often see less use, maintenance intervals tend to be farther apart. Typical maintenance would include changing oil, checking the air filter and changing it if needed, changing the fuel filter if so equipped, and checking the spark plug.

The best source of specific maintenance and troubleshooting information for your generator is the owner’s manual.

#6332. A Black Hole Smaller Than an Atom Could Trigger One of the Universe’s Most Violent Explosions

An ancient black hole no larger than an atom could consume a star from within and eventually trigger a spectacular explosion. New simulations by physicists at MIT and collaborating institutions suggest that these events could produce detectable bursts of radiation, offering a possible way to discover black holes formed shortly after the Big Bang.

The findings, published in The Astrophysical Journal, could also help scientists investigate dark matter, the invisible substance that makes up most of the universe’s matter.

Primordial black holes may have formed when exceptionally dense regions collapsed under gravity during the first fraction of a second after the Big Bang. The smallest would have evaporated through Hawking radiation, but heavier examples could survive today. Some might be as small as an atom yet contain the mass of an asteroid (or about a millionth of the mass of the Earth).

The researchers investigated what would happen if one of these black holes encountered a Sun-like star. Although a star’s gravity alone would not capture a passing black hole, interactions involving a companion star or planet could trap it. Repeated passages through the star would gradually reduce its orbital energy, allowing it to settle into the stellar core over thousands to millions of years.

“Then, this is where the action begins,” says lead author Ore Gottlieb, an assistant professor of physics at MIT.

The team’s three-dimensional simulations suggest that a captured black hole could grow by consuming stellar material. Within several million years, it might absorb approximately 1 percent of the star’s mass. If the star rotates fast enough, the remaining gas would form a spinning disk around the black hole.

“Inside the star, you have a black hole with a disk,” Gottlieb says. “The black hole is also spinning, and it’s twisting space and time.”

As material spirals inward, the black hole would twist magnetic fields in the surrounding disk, generating powerful jets capable of tearing through the star.

“Once the disk forms, this is essentially a death sentence for the star,” Gottlieb says.

“This twisted magnetic field will power very strong electromagnetic jets from the poles of the black hole,” Gottlieb explains. “And these jets will just explode the star, within a few dozen seconds. It’s very fast. Once you have a disk, you are done.”

The resulting explosion could produce a brilliant flash of blue and ultraviolet light, along with X-rays and gamma rays. As the event evolves, its emissions would shift across the electromagnetic spectrum.

“We would initially detect some X-rays and gamma rays, then over time optical and infrared emissions, and later on radio emissions,” Gottlieb says. “This is something we could potentially detect, if it’s not happening too far from us. It could be many galaxies away, not just in our backyard.”

Other cosmic explosions can produce similar signals, so astronomers would need additional evidence to identify a primordial black hole. One possible clue would be an explosion involving a star that would not normally be expected to explode.

“For instance, if the star is a certain mass that is not supposed to explode, it must be something that is happening inside that is a sort of parasite that is consuming the star from the inside,” Gottlieb says.

No primordial black hole has yet been confirmed through this mechanism, but the predicted signals could guide future observations.

“There is hope for us to probe primordial black holes through interactions with stars,” Gottlieb says. “We expect this to be visible, and it’s something we should look into.”

“The broader impact is that we can now place constraints on primordial black holes, and their contributions to dark matter, using observations.”

Reference: “The Life and Death of Stars that Capture Primordial Black Holes” by Ore Gottlieb, Matteo Cantiello, Cameron Norton, Ken Van Tilburg and Matthew Kleban, 19 November 2026, The Astrophysical Journal. DOI: 10.3847/1538-4357/aeb7e1

This work was supported, in part, by the U.S. Department of Energy Office of Science Advanced Scientific Computing Research Program, and by the National Science Foundation.

While scientists continue to work with theories, models and simulations, trying to find ways to prove dark matter, I’ve been performing and uploading online videos of cheaply and easily replicated experiments that demonstrate through gravity intensification through rotation/spin that dark matter is not needed to explain observations of stars revolving around their suns more rapidly than expected in the outer regions of spiral galaxies. Even my most recent ad-free video (https://odysee.com/@charlesgshaver:d/5Gravity:c) is more than a year old now. To try to preempt another comment that a published professional peer reviewed study is necessary for scientific acceptance of my lay findings, I’m resorting to paraphrasing an old adage: “A successful demonstration video is worth a thousand professional peer reviews.”

You literally just said “Stars orbiting around their Suns”. So you wonder why people won’t take you seriously do ya?

Joking aside what you need to do if don’t want to be considered some kook on the Internet is to get ahold of someone in the physics department of your local University, ask them nicely if they could look over what you have and tell you what is wrong about it. If there is any merit to your idea they could at least tell you what datasets to go dig through to look for proof.

If there is any merit to your hypothesis then they may even offer to help you collect data or setup an experiment to prove or disprove your hypothesis. That is how science is done. In a boring methodical way where you try to find everything that disproves your idea, then address how your idea survives these apparent contradictions, most likely by setting up an experiment where your idea being true is the only way it could yield the result that you get.

It’s a lot more boring than putting together a website and screaming on Science blogs how you’ve managed to crack a problem that the best minds our species has produced haven’t been able to with billions of dollars and the most sensitive instruments mankind has ever produced.

Scientists are perplexed at discovering the world's deepest explosive volcanic eruption at Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A submersible mission to the deepest ocean trench on Earth has made a shocking discovery: the deepest pyroclastic volcanic flow ever found on the planet, in a place geologists didn't expect to see any volcanic activity.

This evidence of a violent undersea eruption was found 20,000 feet (6,000 meters) below the ocean surface on the walls of the Challenger Deep, the deepest point of the Mariana Trench and the deepest part of the ocean. It was a "complete surprise," said Robert Stern, a professor emeritus of geosciences at the University of Texas at Dallas and first author of a new study describing the discovery.

Typically, volcanic activity doesn't occur that close to an ocean trench, Stern told Live Science. And given the site's extreme depth, the lava that made the flow must have had some very strange chemistry. Normally, the intense pressure of seawater at these depths would prevent an explosive eruption, instead favoring a goopier, seeping type of flow. But the flows seen on the edge of the Challenger Deep were similar to the explosive, roiling gases that coated Pompeii in ash in A.D. 79.

"It's not something that as a geoscientist I would have said would be predicted," said Sune Nielsen, a geochemist at the University of Lorraine in France who was not involved in the study. "Very far from it."

A fish in the genus Pseudoliparis in an image taken during during a dive by the Jason/Medea ROV at 20,659 feet (6,297 m).

The Challenger Deep is in the remote western Pacific at the southern end of the Mariana Trench. There, the Pacific oceanic plate pushes under the Mariana oceanic plate in a process called subduction. At the trench where the two plates meet, the ocean floor plunges down 6.8 miles (10.9 kilometers). Mount Everest could fit in the chasm, with room to spare.

Geoscientists aren't sure why the trench is so dizzyingly deep, but they have turned up some clues. For instance, there is a tear in the Pacific Plate that allows one narrow strip of the plate to subduct particularly rapidly. The curvature of the plate is also very steep, perhaps because the rocks of the Mariana and Pacific plates aren't very strongly connected to each other, allowing the Pacific Plate to dive steeply and flex freely.

The new findings, reported Monday (Nov. 23) in the journal Frontiers in Earth Science, suggest that volcanism and magma also may play a role, Stern said. The researchers were exploring a segment of the Challenger Deep's forearc, a roughly 120-mile-wide (200 km) expanse that sits between the trench itself and the volcanic arc created by the subduction zone. These volcanic arcs are standard subduction zone features; for example, Mount St. Helens and Mount Rainier are part of the volcanic arc of the Cascadia subduction zone in the Pacific Northwest.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

But though there are some volcanoes north of Challenger Deep along the Mariana Trench, the Challenger Deep segment of the trench is odd in that there is not an organized volcanic arc there. Instead, there's an ocean ridge. Regardless, the space between this ridge and the trench was expected to be volcanically quiet because there is not usually enough heat in that region of a subduction zone to melt magma.

Nevertheless, the cameras on the deep-diving remotely operated vehicle Jason/Medea, which went to the site in 2014, caught strange, pancake-like rock features at three different spots in a 60-mile (100 km) stretch of the trench. Samples brought on board the ship revealed rock embedded with volcanic glass and a pyroclastic flow texture.

A sea cucumber in an image from the Jason/Medea dive at 12,726 feet (3879 m).

The researchers are currently getting the rock dated, but volcanic glass usually erodes quickly in the ocean, Stern said, so the presence of glass suggests the eruptions were fairly recent. "They're not yesterday," he said, "but I don't think they're a million years old."

The pressure of the water at the depths of the flows is equivalent to 592 atmospheres of Earth stacked on top of one another. Typically, that kind of pressure keeps a lid on the dissolved water and carbon dioxide in magma that expands rapidly to cause explosive eruptions. Thus, Stern said, the eruptions by the Challenger Deep may have been driven by a supercritical fluid ‪—‬ a weird state sort of in between a gas and a liquid.

"We just don’t know how those magmas will behave at those water depths," said Stephen Self, a volcanologist at the University of California, Berkeley, who was not involved in the study.

The mission's observations also suggest that the crust of this region is extending, or stretching, in two different ways. To the east, the stretch is caused by a mechanical pulling apart of the crust. To the west, volcanic eruptions are stretching the crust. It's a perplexing finding, Nielsen said, without a clear explanation.

Stern and his colleagues suspect that the two plates are starting a new subduction zone in this western part. That would be an exciting finding; subduction zones move around over tens of millions of years, and researchers don't know much about how new ones start. The geochemical studies of the rocks that Stern and his team pulled up could answer questions about where the lava that made the pyroclastic flows came from and why this bizarre region can generate magma where none should be.

"This region is really, really unusual for our planet, and there is quite a bit of, 'What, really? Wait, how is that? OK, yeah, I guess maybe.'" Nielsen said. "So obviously, I find it super interesting."

Stern, R. J., Pujana, I., Anderson, M. K., Chin, E., Dygert, N., Harigane, Y., Le Roux, V., Leybourne, M., Ohara, Y., Okumura, T., Segee-Wright, G., & Etheridge, E. (n.d.). ROVing in the deep: Tectonic and magmatic complexities of the challenger deep forearc segment, southern mariana convergent margin. Frontiers in Earth Science, 14, 1929806. https://doi.org/10.3389/feart.2026.1929806

#6330. BepiColombo Captures Mercury Orbit After 8-Year Trip

The planet Mercury might be one of the least explored planetary bodies in the solar system, but its is arguably the most crucial in helping scientists better understand the formation and evolution of the inner solar system. Its position as the closest planet to the Sun makes it a prime target for how the rocky planets formed and evolved and what this could mean for finding life beyond Earth. However, just traveling to Mercury is a lengthy and time-consuming effort, often taking a spacecraft several years just to achieve orbit. More on that later.

Now, the lauded joint mission between the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) called BepiColombo might have just become the second mission to orbit Mercury. This is because mission leaders recently announced that BepiColombo successfully achieved Mercury orbit insertion (MOI) on November 21 at 18:27 UTC (1:27 pm EST/10:27 am PST). This historic achievement comes 8 years, 1 month, and 1 day since BepiColombo launched on October 20, 2018, and included one Earth flyby, two Venus flybys, and six mercury flybys to achieve orbit just a few days ago.

While MOI is essential for achieving Mercurian orbit, it is not the final orbit BepiColombo will achieve to conduct science operations, which are expected to commence in April 2027. Over the next several months, the team will fire the spacecraftâs thrusters several times to adjust its orbit to achieve a more permanent orbit. The first science operations phase is slated to run from April 2027 to April 2028 with a potential extended mission from April 2028 to December 2029. If the mission is extended until December 2029, the team will then assess the spacecraftâs remaining fuel and determine if continued science operations can be achieved or if it will crash into Mercuryâs surface.

âOur almost 600-strong science team will be delighted to see BepiColombo pass this key milestone and begin revealing more about Mercury, from its interior and surface to the space around it,â said Dr. Geraint Jones, who is the Lead Project Scientist for ESAâs BepiColombo and was previously was a Professor of Planetary Science and Head of the Planetary Science Group at University College London's Mullard Space Science Laboratory (UK).

As noted, BepiColombo just became the second mission to successfully orbit Mercury, with the first being NASAâs MESSENGER (MErcury Surface, Space ENvironment, GEochemistry, and Ranging) spacecraft, which orbited Mercury from March 2011 to April 2015 after initial estimates put the science phase of the mission lasting only one year. During this time, MESSENGER completed more than 4,100 orbits around the innermost planet to the Sun while obtaining almost 300,000 images of the entire Mercurian surface before its fuel was exhausted. Once this happened, the mission team intentionally crashed MESSENGER into the planetâs far side with the team confirming a loss of signal when the spacecraft was scheduled to emerge from the far side.

Unlike MESSENGER, BepiColombo consists of two orbiters, ESAâs Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXAâs Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter ("Mio"), which are currently attached but are slated to separate in early December 2026. Once this happens, MPO will be tasked with studying Mercury surface features and composition while Mio will study Mercuryâs magnetic field and how it interacts with the solar wind.

As noted earlier, traveling to Mercury is a lengthy and time-consuming effort. This is because as an object travels closer to the Sun, our starâs immense gravity becomes greater, thus increasing the speed of the object. In the case of a spacecraft, this means it has to slow down enough to enter orbit around Mercury. However, this would require an insane amount of fuel, which adds weight to the spacecraft, and the financial and logistical costs spiral from there. This is why spacecraft like BepiColombo and MESSENGER conducted several planetary flybys to slow down, with MESSENGER performing three less mercury flybys compared to BepiColomboâs six Mercury flybys.

What new insights about Mercury will BepiColombo teach scientists in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!

As always, keep doing science & keep looking up!

#6329. Astronomers Discover the Sun Contains 55% More Silver Than Previously Thought

Some of the oldest rocks in the solar system hinted that astronomers were undercounting the Sun’s silver. A fresh look at sunlight suggests they were right.

Researchers at Uppsala University estimate that silver is 55 percent more abundant in the Sun than previous calculations indicated.

The revised estimate brings the Sun much closer to the silver abundance found in primitive meteorites. Both preserve material from the same cloud of gas and dust that gave rise to the solar system 4.6 billion years ago.

Silver atoms in the Sun’s atmosphere absorb light at specific wavelengths, leaving dark lines in the spectrum. The pattern identifies silver, but estimating how much is there requires a model that predicts how strongly those atoms absorb light.

The team modeled the motion of the Sun’s outer layers and used more detailed calculations of how silver atoms interact with light and other particles. The model accounts for how radiation changes the energy states of silver atoms, which affects the strength of the lines astronomers use to measure the element’s abundance.

“With our new model, we were able to interpret the spectral lines used to determine the solar silver abundance more accurately,” says Sema Caliskan, who conducted the research during her PhD studies at Uppsala University.

Hydrogen and helium make up nearly all of the Sun. Heavier elements such as carbon, iron, and silver account for just 1.5 percent of its mass. Many of these elements form inside stars or during stellar explosions, then become part of later generations of stars and planets. Measuring their abundance helps astronomers reconstruct how the Milky Way’s chemistry changed over time.

“The new knowledge about the Sun’s composition is important for the understanding of other stars, planets, and cosmic material, because the Sun is one of astronomy’s key reference points,” says Caliskan.

The team plans to apply the same method to other stars. “By studying the light of stars of different types and ages, we hope to understand where silver is formed in the universe, and how it has been distributed throughout the Milky Way over time,” says Caliskan.

Reference: “Ag I model atom and the 3D non-LTE solar silver abundance” by S. Caliskan, A. M. Amarsi, P. Jönsson, N. Grevesse and B. K. Sahoo, 17 July 2026, Astronomy & Astrophysics. DOI: 10.1051/0004-6361/202659578

This study was funded by the Swedish Research Counsil, KVA Kungliga vetenskapsakademien, and ANRF India.

#6328. NASA’s Giant Pressure Cooker Reveals How Venus Hides Clues to Its Potential Watery Past

Venus will be drawing a lot of attention in the near future. So far, no spacecraft has survived on its surface for more than a few hours, and that was back in the 1970s and â80s. But a series of new missions coming up should give us a clearer picture of what exactly exists on the surface there. And a new paper, available in The Planetary Science Journal from Sara Taeko Port, a postdoc researcher at the University of Texas San Antonio, provides some clues as to what we would expect to find there, and whether what we do see means there used to be water on our âevil twin.â

Venus itself is largely considered an actual hellscape. Read anything about the planet and you will immediately understand how hostile it is. Temperatures average around 460 degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt lead. The atmospheric pressure is around 93 times what Earthâs average ocean-level pressure is â the equivalent of diving a kilometer into the ocean. Oh, and the air is made of carbon dioxide topped by clouds of sulfuric acid.

While this might sound pretty terrible for humans, for the rocks that make up Venusâ surface, itâs just another day on the planet. But what they are and how they form can give planetary scientists an insight into their history. And what they used to be could provide insight into whether there used to be water on Venusâ surface or not.

Fraser talks about our future exploration of Venus.

To prove this point, Dr. Port and her colleagues turned to the Glenn Extreme Environment Rig (GEER), at NASAâs Glenn Research Center in Cleveland. This specialized test chamber is an 811-liter stainless steel pressure vessel engineered specifically to replicate the temperature, pressure, and chemical mixture of Venusâ lower atmosphere. And itâs one of the only places in the world where those conditions can be found.

The research team put a combination of slabs and powders of three carbonate minerals (siderite, calcite, and magnesite) and three minerals that contain water (phlogopite, brucite, and muscovite). They then turned the chamber on and let the samples sit there for sixty days.

Underpinning this experiment is a theory held by many planetary scientists that Venus used to be much more hospitable. In this theory, it was almost Earth-like at one point, before a runaway greenhouse effect boiled away its oceans. Indeed, clues like a significantly high deuterium/hydrogen ratio in its atmosphere point to the planet losing a massive amount of water over time. So, if there was water on its surface at one point, planetary scientists would expect to find signs of that in the geological record.

Fraser talks about why plate tectonics are so crucial to Venus' environment.

But thereâs a big question mark about whether the minerals formed around liquid water would have survived Venusâ transition to its current state. The planetâs atmosphere, along with what scientists believe to be active volcanoes, is potentially damaging enough that any water-formed minerals could have been drastically changed over the course of the last few billion years. Dr. Port and her colleagues thought the best way to test that would be to watch what happened to actual samples of potential minerals.

The answers to that question were somewhat surprising. Brucite, a magnesium-rich mineral that is formed in liquid water on Earth, dried out, then cracked, and changed into a different mineral called magnesite, a type of tough carbonate mineral. Once that magnesite was formed, though, it didnât change much. This means if a future mission finds magnesite on a Venusian plain, it could be a sign of past water, depending on the surrounding geology since technically magnesite can also form without it.

Another surprise came from a class of materials known as micas. These are flaky, water-bearing materials that usually form in wet volcanic environments and go by names like phlogopite or muscovite. Typically, the extreme heat and sulfur dioxide present on Venus would strip the water molecules out of these minerals, causing them to break down. However, Venusâ atmosphere also contains trace amounts of hydrogen fluoride gas. In the environmental chamber, fluorine atoms swapped out with the water-associated hydroxyl groups in the chemical structure of the minerals, turning them into minerals with even crazier names like fluorophlogopite and fluoromuscovite.

Fraser discusses the oddities of Venus with Dr. Paul Byrne.

That swap also protects the minerals from the heat. Swapping hydroxyl for fluorine boosts a micaâs resistance to high temperatures, allowing it to exist even in the harsh temperatures of Venusâ surface for billions of years. So in this particular case, a toxic gas in Venusâ environment might actually help preserve a mineral that was formed when the planet still had plenty of liquid water.

Speaking of volcanoes, the paper adds yet more evidence that Venus must be currently volcanically active. In the experiment, almost every sample absorbed sulfur or fluorine, forming their respective sulfates, sulfides, and fluorides as a type of outer crust. If that absorption process happened over millions of years (such as the 500-million years since the last major resurfacing event on Venus), calculations in the paper show all of those gases would have vanished from the atmosphere long ago unless something was continuously dumping them back in. The most logical explanation would be volcanoes doing so.

That meshes well with previous missions to Venus â archival radar data from NASAâs Magellan spacecraft revealed that a volcanic vent on Maat Mons, Venusâ tallest volcano, reshaped itself over the course of eight months back in 1991. But there are also plenty more missions to come, including NASAâs DAVINCI and VERITAS and ESAâs EnVision spacecraft. This paper on our sister planetâs mineralogy provides a clear roadmap to what those missionsâ scientists should look for as potential signs of where our two geological paths diverged so drastically.

UT San Antonio - UT San Antonio researchers uncover new clues to understanding Venus

S. T. Port et al - New Insights into Venusâs Volatile Cycles Revealed by the Formation of Magnesite and FluoroâMicas

UT - Scientists Discover New Geological Link Between Earth and Venus

UT - NASA's VERITAS Mission Breathes New Life

#6327. The 8 Best Home Generators Are a Big Investment. These Deliver Reliable Power During an Outage.

Our editor-tested and researched portable and whole-home options keep appliances and other essentials running during an emergency—no matter what.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Stronger and more frequent severe weather events are making a compelling argument for investing in a home generator. A large portable generator or a permanently installed standby generator can keep your entire home powered and operational for several days, or at least keep a few critical appliances such as a refrigerator running until the power comes back on. The cost of emergency power is never a small investment, though it is an increasingly important one.

The term “home generator” can be confusing. It’s an unofficial category that includes larger portable generators capable of powering several appliances or a few critical circuits using a transfer switch (not all portable generators are built for this task). It also includes permanently installed standby generators that can automatically switch to whole-home backup power when the lights go out. Choosing the right size generator primarily comes down to how much power you think you’ll need in an emergency.

There are many reliable home generators that deliver a great deal of power. Some offer you the choice of running on multiple different fuels, while other models use an inverter that can give you quieter and “cleaner” operation. There is a nice range of prices available, too, so you can easily find a generator below that fits your needs as well as your budget.

For the generators on this list that we tested, we considered the difficulty of unboxing, assembling, and starting each generator for the first time, because few things are as frustrating as buying a tool that turns out to be unnecessarily complicated from the get-go.

Once set up, the generators we reviewed were subjected to different load conditions, including things such as power tools, home appliances, and even recharging large power stations. We assessed the features that distinguish these generators from each other, including safety features, app connectivity, and portability, among other things.

A few picks on our list have not been tested, but we included them here after considerable research, taking into account the brand’s reputation, our knowledge of its product lines, various outside reviews, and our own experience testing similar models from those same brands.

The DuroMax XP11000iH is a powerful midsize dual-fuel inverter generator, capable of keeping most homes up and running for an extended period of time. Inverter generators are a step above traditional generators because they convert alternating current (AC) to direct current (DC) and then back again to AC. This process creates cleaner, more efficient power and enables the generator to run more quietly and fuel efficiently.

Having two fuel options—gas and propane—provides a big boost of convenience by allowing you to use whatever’s handy. No gasoline? You can use the same tank of propane you use for your gas grill. It’s also parallel-capable, so you can daisy-chain it with another generator if you need extra power.

The generator is enclosed in a large, sturdy plastic casing, which makes it durable and provides a fair amount of sound dampening. Of the many gas generators I’ve tested, it may be the quietest model that’s capable of backing up a whole home, especially when it’s running on propane, which trims it down by another few decibels. At 61 decibels on a 20 percent load, it’s about as loud as a dishwasher. Most comparably sized generators go up to around 80 decibels—about the same volume as a police siren.

In addition to a full suite of essential modern safety features such as a carbon monoxide shutoff and low-oil shutoff, it goes the extra mile with lots of little touches, like remote start. The integrated battery tender keeps it ready to start, no matter how long it’s been sitting, which can be a lifesaver, too. When you do run out to check it, an onboard display shows you key stats such as hours run, current load, and voltage output.

The only downside I could find was its weight. At upward of 200 pounds, it isn’t easy to carry. It does have wheels and sturdy handles, though, so it isn’t hard to wheel around on flat, paved ground—if you can push a loaded wheelbarrow, you can push this. Not that you’ll need to move it much; it’s a very sturdy generator, and it comes assembled with the wheels and handles attached (not all generators come with those pre-attached). —Reviewed by Nick Hilden

Technically, there are cheaper generators out there, but the Generac GP9500E offers an outstanding blend of capability, quality, and durability at a very reasonable price. As such, this is where I’d steer you if you’re trying to shave down your spend.

Its 9,500-watt running capacity is slightly higher than the DuroMax’s, and it’s capable of powering all but the largest of homes. It can get a little noisy under a heavy load, but that’s common with units this size. It let out a relatively moderate purr when it was just powering the lights and a few appliances, but it became more of a roar when the heat kicked on.

With three fuel options—gas, propane, and natural gas—you get about as much versatility as you could possibly expect from a generator. A relatively large 7.5-gallon gas tank delivers a long runtime between fill-ups. And, while I was initially skeptical as to the necessity of the third fuel option, having natural gas support showed its value when a storm knocked out the power, and I didn’t have gas or propane on hand. All I needed to do was plug it into the natural gas line, and suddenly my house was the only one on the block with lights on.

Beyond that, though, it’s a fairly basic model. It has essential safety features such as low-oil and CO shutdown, but lacks elements such as a fancy digital display, remote start, or app. I don’t necessarily think that’s a problem: It can be helpful to get a piece of machinery that doesn’t go overboard with features. Its control panel is about as straightforward as can be, and it’s a cinch to get up and running.

Like my top pick, the GP9500E is exceedingly heavy. It’s also quite sturdy, though, which feels like a fair trade. The outlet covers aren’t as flimsy and breakable as with many other models of a similar price point. It isn’t completely immobile: It has wheels and handles that make it easy to cart around short distances. Realistically, though, weight is almost always going to be an issue with any generator capable of backing up your house.

Ultimately, its selling point is the price. It’s hard to find a quality tri-fuel generator for around $1,100, and the GP9500E performs well if you don’t mind losing out on some bells and whistles.

Whether you’re connecting devices individually, powering an RV, or running home backup power during a storm, this generator from Westinghouse (model WGen9500DF) covers all the bases. In addition to being dual-fuel (gas or propane), it includes both 30- and 50-amp outputs capable of powering 120- and 240-volt circuits. That means you could connect this generator to a transfer switch installed in your home using either option. And with 9,500 running watts of power, it’s enough for several critical circuits in your home, including the ones that run on 240 volts, such as a heating/ventilation/air-conditioning system, electric dryer, or well pump.

Several other features caught our attention, including a push-button electric start and stop (no need to mess with a pull cable), plus a remote start key fob. There’s an automatic low-oil shutoff, and the display provides the voltage output, frequency, and lifetime hours (this can run up to 12 hours on a 6.6-gallon tank of gasoline). The only drawback is the 74-decibel noise level. While that’s typical of generators of this type, if you're planning on using this to power an RV or camper, it may be too loud for some parks, as many limit generator noise to under 70 decibels.

While it does not offer as much power as some of the choices on our list, Champion’s 4,750-watt generator has enough capacity to run three or four critical 120-volt circuits in your home during an outage. It will also power small to medium campers and RVs via a dedicated 30-amp, 120-volt RV receptacle. Listed at around $600, this generator gives you a lot for the price you pay.

This generator uses a 224-cc engine with a 4.7-gallon fuel tank, enabling it to run for up to 14 hours (up to 10 hours using propane). A gauge displays a readout of the runtime hours and voltage output, and there’s an automated shutoff feature if the oil starts to run low. Since it’s dual-fuel, this generator can run off propane in addition to gasoline. For instance, if you are using it with an RV, you can run it off a camper’s propane tank without having to pack and haul a gas can. Likewise, with the included adapter hose, you can hook it up to a 20-pound propane tank.

There are a few drawbacks. Beyond the somewhat low wattage output for whole-home backup, there are no 240-volt outlets, so if you need that many volts to power circuits in your home for something such as a dryer or water heater, this model won’t be right for you. But if you just need something to keep some lights on and run a few appliances, this generator will get the job done and not cost you a ton of money up front to do it. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford

There are many reasons to opt for an inverter generator, but the two biggest ones are: cleaner, more stable power (important for powering electronics safely) and less noise. Loudness becomes a major factor with larger generators, as more power requires a more powerful engine. That’s why we were so impressed with this model (EU7000iS) from Honda. It delivers a lot of power but at notably low loudness levels.

It’s important to note that this is not a small generator. It weighs in at 263 pounds, making it one of the heaviest on our list. That said, we found it fairly comfortable to move around. The metal frame that houses the generator has a folding handle that locks into place and is capped with soft grips, while on the front of the frame there are strong 10-inch rubber wheels. This made it fairly easy to roll around, even up some gradual slopes.

It’s also quite sturdy. The outer casing is constructed of stamped metal and impact-resistant composite hard plastic, with two large, hinged maintenance doors that lock into place.

Once we fired up the generator, it was noticeably quieter than other models we’ve tested, even when outputting a 60 percent load. Using an app-based sound meter, we were reading around 70 decibels from 15 feet away, which is lower than you would see with a non-inverter generator. This is helped by an “Eco Throttle” mode that adjusts the engine speed to meet demand as different devices are added, but we found even the standard throttle mode was fairly quiet as well.

Other things we liked were an app that allows for remote operation over Bluetooth, ground fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) protection, a carbon monoxide (CO) sensor, and 240-volt output over a 30-amp connection, which will let the generator connect to a manual transfer switch for sending direct power to your home electrical box.

The two downsides are the cost (it’s very expensive at more than $4,000) and the fact that it can only be powered by gasoline; Honda doesn’t offer dual- or tri-fuel models for using propane or natural gas. But if those two considerations don’t bother you, the EU7000iS Inverter Generator is a high-quality machine that will keep you more quietly powered than some of the competition.

Full Honda EU7000iS 7000-Watt Inverter Generator Review

Battery-based backup systems are getting smarter and more powerful every year, making them an increasingly strong contender to fuel-based standby generators. This model from EcoFlow is one of the most powerful we’ve tested.

The power station combines a separate inverter unit with two 6-kilowatt-hour batteries for a total of 12-kilowatt-hour capacity. That’s enough to run power-hungry devices simultaneously—things such as heating/ventilation/air-conditioning systems, electric ovens and dryers, microwaves, and air-conditioning units. Add to this increased solar input, and you can recharge faster, too. For our tests, we connected this to a home electrical system in the home using EcoFlow’s Smart Home Panel 3, which acts as the automatic transfer switch.

During testing, our reviewer experienced two power outages, one for a few seconds and one for several minutes. This power station features an Emergency Power Supply (EPS) mode, which facilitates a 20-millisecond switch to backup power—without this set, it normally switches in about five seconds. During the longer outage, the switch from grid to backup power, and then back again, was seamless. It was fast enough that the lights never flickered and the internet never dropped.

Several advanced smart features stand out. The smartphone app enables you to view power usage, down to the circuit, preset what circuits get backup power during outages, manually turn circuits on and off, and schedule automated tasks such as charging and discharging. You’ll also receive notifications when the grid goes down and the backup power takes over. If you live in an area where electricity is cheaper during low-peak hours, it can also prioritize recharging from grid power by choosing those times of day.

Meanwhile, this system is highly expandable. You can add up to eight more batteries for a total of 10, and an inlet box that comes with the smart panel has three ports. You could plug a Delta Pro Ultra X, bolstered by extra batteries, into each port to increase the total energy storage up to a whopping 184.3 kilowatt-hours of capacity and 36 kilowatts of continuous output.

One of the biggest things our reviewer appreciates about the Delta Pro Ultra X and Smart Home Panel 3 is the peace of mind it gives. If the grid goes down, they know that their home systems will continue to run. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford

When AC power isn’t available, the greenest way to recharge a power station is with solar panels. However, the panel’s maximum power output often exceeds the maximum solar input, so they just can’t recharge fast enough. In these cases, whole-home, battery-based backup systems need the help of a fuel-based generator to recharge, so you’re not left high and dry if the power’s still out. That’s where the EcoFlow Smart Generator 4000 comes in.

This dual-fuel (gas or propane) generator connects to select EcoFlow power stations via a DC charging and communication cable, including the Delta Pro, Delta Pro 3, Delta 3, Delta 3 Plus, and Delta 2 Max. (Note: If your preferred brand is Anker, it also makes a fuel generator that’s compatible with some of its power stations, the 5500 Tri-Fuel Inverter Generator, which we also tested and reviewed.) This DC connection allows autonomous operation, so when a station’s battery hits critically low levels, the generator automatically starts to recharge it.

You can also recharge non-DC-compatible power stations by simply plugging them into the AC output, though it’s a slower recharge. If it’s an EcoFlow station, you can still automate startup, too, by pairing over Bluetooth. But you won’t be able to do this with other brands of power stations.

Our test editor Bradley Ford noted that EcoFlow’s app is one of the best features of this generator. Connecting over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, he used it to monitor fuel consumption and output, as well as set automated functions. He also tested how it can set the charging speed, monitor power output, and schedule times to start and stop the generator. He especially liked that the app provides a lot of useful information as well, such as generator fuel usage and estimated runtime.

Of course, it can work as a standalone generator, too, though there are some limitations. Ford notes that there are only two outlets: a 120-volt, 20-amp outlet and a 120-volt, 30-amp outlet. The latter outlet can connect to a manual transfer switch installed in your home, but it won’t be able to power any 240-volt circuits, and the total output of 3,200 watts is only enough to power a few circuits. However, he thinks it would work well for RV use, and because it’s an inverter generator, it’s better at safely powering sensitive electronics like TVs and computers. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford

Full EcoFlow Dual-Fuel Smart Generator 4000 Review

Pulsar is a relatively new brand in the generator business and doesn’t have a long track record. We first spotted it on Amazon and didn’t seriously consider its generators for testing. That was, up until our test editor needed a generator (with specific features and on a budget) after a generator failed at his solar-powered off-grid cabin. Happily, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel Inverter Generator showed up quickly and didn’t disappoint.

The generator was easy to assemble and prep, taking only 15 minutes. After adding oil, it was connected to a propane cylinder and was up and running on the first cycle of the starter. Our first task was to charge a solar battery bank during a wintertime period when there was not enough available sunlight, and it worked perfectly.

We have logged more than 20 hours of use so far, running it primarily on propane connected to a 100-pound cylinder (enough fuel to last a couple of months). This Pulsar puts out very clean power, with a claimed total harmonic distortion (THD) of less than 3 percent, which met the requirements of the solar inverter-charger I was using. Using the inverter to monitor the current frequency, we found that it was indeed very stable with minimal variance, between 59.97 and 60.09 Hz. All things considered, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel is a good value for the specs, capacity, and features. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford

True whole-home backup requires a professionally installed standby generator like Generac’s 22-kilowatt home standby generator. It’s designed to power a house that’s roughly 2,500 square feet. If you need to run specialized medical devices, work from home, or have kids who are learning from home, this model is a sound investment.

Another benefit of this bundle is that it includes a transfer switch, which is required if you’re planning to install this type of generator. It supports 200-amp electrical service, providing the backup circuits needed to power high-voltage appliances such as refrigerators and well pumps, along with air conditioning and heating systems. Plus, there’s built-in WiFi for checking the status of your generator and receiving maintenance alerts when you’re not at home.

You could just drive over to your local hardware store and buy a large portable generator to use as a home backup, but we wouldn’t recommend it. You want to make sure you’re getting a generator that can back up your home and power all the appliances, lights, and electronics inside. (Plus some extra watts in case you need them down the line.)

In addition, there are often state and local laws or homeowners association rules and restrictions around using them in residential neighborhoods. Choosing poorly or setting up your backup generator incorrectly could damage the generator or short out your house power at best, or lead to fire, electrocution, or carbon monoxide poisoning at worst.

Picking the best generator for your home starts with a little math. Ideally, you want to calculate how much energy you need to keep your house running, and buy a generator that can handle everything you want to power in an emergency, with room to spare.

The two key specs to pay attention to are the running wattage and starting wattage (e.g., 9,500 running watts / 12,500 starting watts). Running wattage is effectively your generator’s capacity: It tells you how much power a generator can produce steadily without any possibility of an overload. Starting wattage is the generator’s max output, or how much power it can produce for short, peak bursts when appliances first switch on.

When you are making your list, note what items are 120-volt and which ones are 240-volt appliances. It’s not hard to identify them. Refrigerators, small appliances, and most electronics run on 120-volt power and plug into standard outlets. Anything that requires 240 volts—electric dryers, well pumps, and HVAC systems—is either hardwired into your electrical system or has a dedicated 240-volt outlet. If you need to power the latter, the installation of a transfer switch and a generator that outputs at least 30 amps/240 volts may be required.

If you’re just looking to keep the fridge, lights, and a few modest appliances going through a short blackout, you can usually get away with a generator that supplies 3,000 to 5,000 watts. If you want to run the heat, hot water, and several appliances at once, plan on using at least 6,000 to 8,000 watts. If you think you’re going to be adding large appliances such as laundry machines and dishwashers, expect to need 10,000 watts or more.

A piece of advice we have: Once you figure out how much you need, opt for buying a generator that outputs around 20 percent more than that. It’s not uncommon to realize you need more than you thought you would.

It’s also important to consider that, while generators are certainly a hefty investment, they usually stand the test of time. Consumer-grade portable generators can run anywhere from 1,000 to 3,000 hours, sometimes more. If you run one for 100 hours per year, it should last for 10 to 30 years.

There are four basic types of generators, each with advantages and disadvantages.

The most traditional of the generator category, these run on carbon-based fuels like gasoline, propane, and natural gas. Some allow you to switch between them. Dual-fuel models add the option of either propane or natural gas, while tri-fuel versions offer all three fuel options. These generators can be small, offering as little as 1,000 watts of power output, or run very large, as much as 20,000 watts or more.

Different fuels offer different power capabilities. For example, a tri-fuel generator may offer 9,500 running watts and 12,500 starting watts with gasoline, but only 8,500/11,200 with propane and 7,500/9,500 with natural gas. Regardless of the fuel you choose, this type of generator must always be operated 5 to 20 feet away from the home or any window or door, because the carbon monoxide exhaust is deadly. Even a garage with an open door is not safe.

Often this type of generator is called portable, but that's a relative term: Almost all of them weigh more than 100 pounds, and many are upwards of 200. Many are on wheels, making them relatively easy to store in a garage and wheel outside when you need them, but actually moving one will likely require at least two people.

Inverter generators look and operate the same as other portable generators, but have an added component–a power inverter– that converts the alternating current (AC) power generated by its fuel source to DC (Direct Current), then inverts it back to AC before putting it out.

Generators without an inverter generate varying degrees of distortion in the sine wave of the alternating current, which can trigger power surges and other issues in some electronics. The inverter stabilizes the power, almost like a filter, “cleaning” it for more sensitive electronics like TVs and laptops.

So why doesn’t every generator have an inverter? Inverters are expensive, so the generators are, too.

Realistically speaking, you don’t need an inverter generator to power major appliances and your house power, but if you’re running a full home backup (or if you count a TV or laptop among your essential electronics), holding out for an inverter is a smart move.

While often referred to as “solar generators” because they can be paired with solar panels, power stations are not really true generators. They're advanced battery banks that store power, which you precharge using AC power or solar panels. They can’t generate electricity in real time.

But because they can offer many of the same electrical outputs as a fuel generator, they can function similarly to a traditional generator for as long as the batteries retain a charge. Some stations are very small and meant only for off-grid adventures like camping trips, but some are large enough to run whole-home systems that can produce 14,400 watts or more with expandable batteries.

Since power stations don't run on fuel or have an engine, they can be used indoors without the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning and operate with almost no noise.

The downside is that once the power is depleted, the power station must be recharged. If the power grid is still unavailable, it can take many hours in ideal sunny conditions if all you have are solar panels. You can use a traditional generator to recharge a power station, but some may view that as defeating the purpose.

Standby generators are permanently installed generators designed to automatically take over for your house power in the event of an outage. You can set them to power your whole house, or only specific circuits, giving you precise control. Standby generators start at around 10,000 watts (10 kilowatts) but can go up to much higher. For the average home, a range of 10 to 25 kilowatts is usually enough.

They typically require professional installation, making them the most costly option. Since many large portable generators can effectively back up a house for a few hours for a lot less money, standby models are still considered a more niche option.

When you draw too much power from your generator, its performance will start to decline. At home, your lights will start to dim or flicker, and appliances may turn off momentarily. The generator itself may also start to get louder, or sound like it’s working extra hard to keep up.

If you notice these signs, start turning off and unplugging non-essential power sources immediately, or turn the generator off entirely for ten minutes or so to reduce the power load.

This is an urgent problem, so do not wait to take action: If you overwork your generator for too long, it’s only a matter of time before it starts to overheat, produce smoke, or break down. The damage from an extended overload could permanently damage the generator or, worse, start a fire.

With the right size for your home, a portable or standby generator can run as long as you keep feeding it fuel and stay within its running wattage capacity; however, you should not run them indefinitely. Manufacturers recommend you allow them to rest for 30 minutes or more after at least 24 hours of use. Check the manual of your generator for its specific recommendations.

You will get more time from each tank of gas if you draw less power, so it helps to pay extra attention to your electricity usage when you’re running the generator.

Make sure to turn your gas and/or propane generators off when it’s time to refill the tank. Failing to do so could lead to a fire.

Power stations, since they rely on electricity or solar power, can almost always be charged while in use.

Never run a fuel-based generator (gasoline, propane, natural gas) indoors. Burning fuel releases carbon monoxide (CO), which will quickly build up to deadly levels in an enclosed space.

Set your generator up outside, between 5 and 20 feet away from your home and/or any garages, sheds, or other walls. Position it as far as possible from doors, windows, and vents, with the exhaust positioned away from the house, to minimize the possibility of fumes wafting in. If you keep it outside all year round, find a naturally covered position where snow won’t naturally pile up around it.

My generator is situated near my home’s power box, which is located on a windowless side of my home. It stands about five feet from the exterior wall, with plenty of space on all sides, but close enough to sit under the roof peak overhang 20 feet above.

David is a Reviews Editor for Hearst’s Enthusiast Group, contributing to Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, Best Products, and Biography. #6325. New Technology Could Help Astronauts Make Their Own Oxygen on the Moon

Astronauts on the Moon could one day breathe oxygen pulled from lunar soil using a technique borrowed from chipmaking.

Computer chip manufacturing and lunar exploration seem like completely different worlds. Yet our latest research suggests the two may be more closely connected than expected.

Using technology widely employed in semiconductor manufacturing, we have shown that it is possible to extract oxygen and products containing oxygen from material designed to mimic lunar soil.

This matters because oxygen is one of the most valuable resources for future space exploration. Astronauts need it to breathe, and it is also a major component of rocket propellant.

But transporting large quantities from Earth would be enormously expensive, so space agencies are investigating ways to obtain it directly on the Moon instead.

The challenge is that lunar oxygen does not exist as a readily available gas. Instead, it is chemically bound within minerals that make up the Moon’s surface layer. And although that layer contains a large amount of oxygen by weight, extracting it requires breaking strong chemical bonds within lunar minerals.

Many of the complex techniques that could potentially achieve this extraction would require large amounts of energy.

So our team decided to explore an alternative, lower-temperature approach inspired by a well-established industrial technology called “plasma-processing.”

Plasma is often called the fourth state of matter (after solid, liquid, and gas). It forms when sufficient energy is supplied to a gas, creating a mixture of charged particles, electrons, and highly reactive chemical species.

In semiconductor fabrication, plasma interacts with silicon dioxide in a process that underpins the production of billions of electronic devices every year.

We asked a simple question: if plasmas are highly effective at reacting with compounds containing oxygen in semiconductor processing, could a similar approach be applied to the oxygen-based compounds in lunar soil?

To investigate, we exposed artificial moon soil (known as lunar regolith simulants) to plasmas generated using gases that are commonly employed in semiconductor manufacturing.

The results were encouraging. During plasma treatment of the lunar regolith simulants, we detected oxygen and oxygen-containing gaseous products being released.

Further analyses confirmed that the plasma was chemically modifying oxygen-bearing minerals within the material, with some lunar minerals reacting more readily than others.

Understanding these underlying mechanisms is important for enhancing the efficiency of the process and identifying opportunities to improve future systems. But oxygen yields would need to increase substantially before any practical lunar system becomes possible.

One reason this approach is attractive is that it builds on decades of experience developed by the semiconductor industry. Space engineering often requires entirely new technologies, but there are advantages in adapting systems that already exist, are well-understood, and have been refined for years on Earth.

The semiconductor industry has spent decades studying how fluorine plasmas interact with materials containing oxygen. Rather than starting from scratch, future researchers can draw on that extensive knowledge base.

There are practical benefits too. Plasma processing is a dry process, avoiding some of the challenges associated with transporting and handling liquid reagents (chemicals added to the process to make a reaction occur) in space. The operating temperatures of plasma processing can also be significantly lower than those required by some conventional oxygen extraction methods.

The implications may extend beyond using oxygen for life support on lunar bases. Lunar soil contains useful elements, including silicon, aluminum, and iron. While our current work focused on oxygen-bearing reactions, future studies may explore whether plasma-based processes could contribute more broadly to the use of other lunar resources.

Much more research is needed to understand the chemistry, to improve yields, and to determine whether the process can be scaled economically.

But the plasma technology that enables the manufacture of billions of transistors may also help humanity tackle one of the biggest challenges of space exploration: learning how to live off the land on another world.

Reference: “Impact of oxygen extraction from lunar regolith simulant using fluorinated plasma processes” by Aneeta Jaggernauth, Sean Kelly, Brian K. Tanner, Robert O’Connor, Aidan Cowley and Rajani K. Vijayaraghavan, 2 September 2026, Scientific Reports. DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-67891-2
