#6269. Scientists discover an unexpected connection between boredom and poor sleep

People who are prone to boredom report greater difficulty falling asleep and poorer sleep quality, even after accounting for mental health factors.

A tendency to get bored easily has been linked to excessive smartphone use and mental health problems. Poor sleep may also belong on that list.

Psychologists in Canada surveyed 565 university students about boredom and their sleeping habits. Those who got bored more easily took longer to fall asleep and generally felt they hadn’t slept well.

The researchers initially considered whether this had something to do with poor self-control, depression or anxiety. But none of these factors fully explained what they were seeing.

James Danckert, a psychology professor at the University of Waterloo, led the study.

His earlier research has explored why boredom prompts some people to find something to do while others struggle to get past the feeling.

“For most people, boredom can serve as a call to action,” Danckert said.

“But for people who suffer from chronic boredom, it’s very difficult to take action and can have a range of negative outcomes, from higher rates of depression and anxiety to increased drug and alcohol use, problem gambling, and problematic smartphone use.”

Danckert and his colleagues surveyed 256 students before repeating much of the study with another 309. The students were around 20 years old on average, and most were women.

Anyone who reported taking sleeping medication was excluded.

To get a sense of how frequently the students experienced boredom, the team asked them how much they agreed with statements such as “Many things I have to do are repetitive and monotonous.”

Some people experience boredom far more readily than others, even when there are things available for them to do. Psychologists refer to this tendency as boredom proneness.

The students had to think back over the previous month and recall how they had been sleeping.

Among other things, the researchers wanted to know how long it typically took them to fall asleep and whether they frequently woke up at night.

There was also a questionnaire about putting off bedtime.

Students rated statements such as “I go to bed later than I had intended.” Separate questionnaires covered depression, anxiety and self-control.

Students who scored high on the boredom questionnaire generally scored poorly on self-control. They also reported more symptoms of depression and anxiety.

These findings were largely in keeping with what psychologists already knew about boredom.

Sleep, however, was a little more complicated.

Even when the researchers accounted for age, gender, mental health symptoms and self-control, they could still see a moderate connection between boredom and poor sleep in both groups.

For some students, the difficulties extended into the following day.

In the second group, problems getting through the day after a bad night’s sleep had a particularly strong association with boredom.

Back in 2021, a study of 270 people found that those who got bored easily often had trouble paying attention and tended to delay going to bed. Both habits were linked to their sleeping difficulties.

Danckert’s team thought bedtime might be worth looking into further.

Students in both groups frequently stayed up later than planned if they were prone to boredom.

But after the researchers took self-control and other factors into consideration, the association held up in only the second group.

The team couldn’t establish why the results differed. There may have been something about the students in each group that the questionnaires failed to capture.

An unpleasant conversation from earlier in the day can be surprisingly hard to put out of one’s mind at night.

Going over upsetting experiences repeatedly is known as rumination. Previous research has found that people who do this before bedtime often lie awake for longer.

The second group of students answered questions about this habit, including how often they “Think about a recent situation, wishing it had gone better.”

Taken together, boredom proneness and rumination explained 13.8% of the variation in sleep quality among students. Clearly, there was more going on than the two questionnaires could account for.

An interesting detail emerged when the researchers asked students how bored they felt while filling out the questionnaires.

One of the statements they rated was “Time is dragging on.”

These temporary feelings of boredom had much the same association with poor sleep as the tendency to experience boredom regularly.

However, students who felt bored at the time of the survey were more likely to dwell on negative thoughts.

The relationship could run in the opposite direction. After a particularly bad night, even activities that people normally enjoy might seem unappealing.

Unfortunately, the way the study was conducted made it impossible to tell which came first. The students filled out the questionnaires on a single occasion.

The researchers suggested having people keep daily records of their sleep and boredom over a longer period. That would give them a better idea of how the two change in relation to each other.

University students aren’t necessarily representative of the wider population. Their sleeping habits can change considerably throughout the academic year, especially when exams are approaching.

Nor did the researchers know exactly how much sleep each student got. They relied entirely on students’ recollections rather than monitoring their sleep.

One questionnaire about sleep habits also had slightly lower reliability than researchers would normally consider acceptable.

Danckert and his colleagues would like to see the research repeated in a more representative group, as well as among people living with depression or anxiety.

For someone who struggles with boredom, even the small tasks involved in getting ready for bed may require considerable effort. Being tired at the end of the day probably doesn’t help.

There is also the temptation to pick up a phone. Someone looking for relief from boredom may end up spending much of the evening online, although the researchers did not investigate this possibility directly.

Despite years of research into boredom and its consequences, psychologists still know relatively little about how to help people who experience it regularly.

What one person finds meaningful or enjoyable may hold very little appeal for another.

The researchers suggest that working on sleep habits might be a more manageable place to start.

Whether better sleep actually makes people less susceptible to boredom remains to be seen.

The study is published in the journal Personality and Individual Differences.

A woman's heart issues seemed to be tied to her rapid gulping of ice-cold drinks.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The patient: A 46-year-old woman in California

The symptoms: After an uneventful 10-hour work shift, the woman was walking to her car and drinking an ice-cold beverage when a sudden, burning pain struck the middle of her chest. The pain spread to both of her forearms and lasted about 20 minutes.

About 10 minutes after this pain began, she started sweating and felt nauseated and lightheaded, as though she might pass out.

What happened next: The pain continued as the woman began driving home, so she changed course and instead drove to the nearest emergency department.

An electrocardiogram (EKG), which records the heart's electrical activity, showed subtle abnormalities. A blood test for troponin, a protein released into the bloodstream when heart muscle is damaged, was normal. However, a second troponin test taken before she left the hospital came back elevated after she had been discharged. Doctors called her about the new results and advised her to drive to the nearest emergency department.

There, a third blood test showed that her troponin level had risen even further, and doctors diagnosed a heart attack. An angiogram — a scan that shows the structure of blood vessels — revealed a small tear in a branch of her right coronary artery, which supplies blood to the heart.

About 30 hours after she was discharged, the woman developed similar chest pain after taking several gulps of ice-cold green tea and subsequently jogging up a flight of stairs. The pain began when she reached the top of the stairs and was accompanied by the same lightheaded feeling she had experienced before.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

She called 911 and was again brought to an emergency department, and although an initial EKG showed no clear signs of a heart attack, subsequent recordings revealed heart-activity changes consistent with one. A second angiogram revealed a new tear in the left circumflex artery, a branch of the left coronary artery.

The woman developed tears in both her right and left coronary arteries, which supply the heart with oxygen-rich blood.

The diagnosis: Doctors diagnosed the woman with spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD), a condition in which a tear develops in the wall of a coronary artery. In SCAD, blood collects within the artery wall, and this compresses the channel that blood normally flows through to reach the heart. As in the patient's case, this compression can sometimes trigger heart attacks by drastically restricting the heart's blood supply.

Doctors also found fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) in a blood vessel in the woman's pelvis. FMD changes the structure of artery walls, making them too weak or too stiff, and it's known to occur in some people with SCAD. It may have made her arteries more prone to tearing, the doctors wrote in a report of the case.

The treatment: During her first emergency department visit, doctors gave the woman aspirin, fluids, medicine for nausea and an antacid. Her chest pain eventually went away. At the second visit, doctors gave her the blood thinner heparin to reduce blood clotting and the beta-blocker metoprolol to slow her heart rate. She was discharged the following morning with prescriptions for cholesterol- and blood-pressure-lowering drugs.

After the second episode, doctors gave her opioid painkillers and medicine for nausea to take as needed, along with aspirin and a cholesterol-lowering drug. The cholesterol-lowering drug was soon stopped because she did not have high cholesterol. Doctors eventually stopped the blood-pressure medication, too, after a follow-up heart ultrasound showed that the affected part of her heart was moving normally again.

She continued taking nebivolol, a different beta-blocker that slows the heart rate and can reduce stress on the organ, for years after these two episodes. And for several months after the second episode, the woman avoided cold drinks on her own initiative. She gradually reintroduced them, taking small sips rather than gulping. Ten years later, she remained free of symptoms, the report noted.

What makes this case unique: Years later, the woman learned that cold drinks had been linked to atrial fibrillation (AFib), an irregular heart rhythm. She told her healthcare team that she suspected cold drinks might have triggered SCAD in her case, too.

Separately, a 2017 case report described another woman who developed chest pain and a heart attack after drinking cold water. Doctors subsequently found that she had SCAD and FMD. However, that report did not investigate cold water as a possible trigger of the patient's symptoms.

The authors of the current report proposed that rapidly swallowing a cold drink may trigger a brief rise in blood pressure, known as a pressor response. This is associated with increased activation of the body's fight-or-flight system, which can then release stress hormones. These changes may make the heart contract more forcefully and cause the coronary arteries to narrow temporarily, thereby increasing the forces acting on their walls. In someone whose arteries are susceptible to tears, that added stress could contribute to rips in the tissue and the accumulation of blood within the artery wall.

However, the report authors stressed that they cannot establish that cold drinks caused the woman's dissections in this instance. They hope their findings will encourage doctors to ask patients with SCAD about potential triggers, but they said further research is needed to determine whether rapidly drinking cold beverages can really trigger the condition.

#6267. One of Earth’s most essential resources has been overlooked by international law

Soil scientists are calling for an international treaty to address land degradation and protect a resource essential to food security and biodiversity.

Some of the phosphorus that nourishes the Amazon rainforest comes from the floor of an ancient lake in Africa.

About 30 million tons of dust blow out of the Sahara Desert and across the Atlantic Ocean every year. When this dust settles over the rainforest, it replenishes nutrients that floods wash out of the ground.

Some 3,100 miles separate the two landscapes, yet the soil in one helps sustain life in the other.

The world has international treaties for the protection of the atmosphere, marine life and biodiversity. Soil, oddly enough, has no treaty of its own.

At the University of Sydney, two soil scientists are making the case for one. In a commentary drawing on earlier research and UN reports, they explain why countries should aim to establish a global soil treaty by 2032.

Much of what scientists know about soil comes from studying how it differs from place to place. There are good practical reasons for doing this, particularly in agriculture.

But Dr. Quentin Styc of the University of Sydney’s School of Life and Environmental Sciences and Sydney Institute of Agriculture sees a problem with this approach.

“We have spent centuries classifying soils according to their different properties, uses and locations. But in doing so, we’ve lost sight of the bigger picture,” said Dr. Styc.

Consider what happens during heavy rain. Water picks up loose soil along with carbon and nutrients, carrying them into streams and rivers, sometimes all the way to the ocean.

What farmers put into the ground can travel considerable distances, too. Excess nitrogen from fertilizers can affect water and air quality far beyond agricultural areas.

According to a 2025 study cited in the commentary, about 7.2% of all pesticides used on land reach groundwater each year. Tiny plastic particles found in soil can travel through the air for up to 500 miles (800 kilometers).

“Soil doesn’t stop functioning at national borders. What happens to soil in one country can have profound consequences for ecosystems, economies and food security on the other side of the world,” said Dr. Styc.

Look through existing international environmental treaties and soil does appear here and there. Much depends, though, on where the soil is located and what purpose it serves.

The United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) comes closest to addressing the problem. Its focus is on drylands, leaving more than 60% of the world’s land outside the main scope of its protection.

Under the international climate treaty, soil matters largely because of how much carbon it can hold.

An estimated 59% of the world’s species live in soil. And while the international biodiversity treaty aims to protect species, it does not offer dedicated protection for soil itself.

Other international guidelines deal with soil management, but governments are under no legal obligation to follow them.

“We have international treaties to protect the ocean and atmosphere. Yet the soil beneath our feet, which is fundamental to human civilisation, remains without equivalent protection,” said Dr. Styc.

“These connections demonstrate why soil security cannot be achieved by countries acting independently,” he said.

In 2017, a group of scientists attempted to calculate the economic value of the world’s soil. Among them was Professor Alex McBratney, the second author of the new commentary.

Their estimate came to about $325 trillion, more than three times the annual output of the global economy.

A great deal of that soil is already in trouble. As much as 40% of the world’s land may be degraded, according to UN figures that the researchers cite.

About $44 trillion in annual economic activity is at risk because of land degradation. That amounts to roughly half of global GDP.

Without action, the UN expects a further $23 trillion in economic losses by 2050.

Then there is the cost of putting things right. Restoring degraded land around the world would require an estimated $4.6 trillion.

The economic stakes are enormous. Earlier research estimated the annual value of the services provided by Earth’s ecosystems at $125 trillion to $145 trillion. Restoring degraded land could help preserve many of these benefits.

The idea of treating a natural resource as something shared by the entire planet is hardly new.

We learn the names of five oceans at school. Yet there is no physical boundary separating these enormous bodies of water from one another.

For years, organizations such as the One Ocean Foundation have encouraged people to think of them as a single ocean.

International law has gradually moved in the same direction. In June 2023, countries adopted the high seas treaty, covering waters beyond national control that account for about 95% of the ocean by volume.

By January 2026, the agreement had come into force after receiving 60 ratifications.

Styc and McBratney are aware of the differences between oceans and soil. There are, for instance, relatively few direct physical connections between soils once distances extend beyond a continent.

But the damage done to soil in one part of the world need not remain there. Air and water provide plenty of ways for its effects to spread.

“We need to think about soil in the singular, just as we increasingly talk about one ocean rather than separate oceans,” said Dr. Styc.

“It’s a change in language that reflects a much bigger change in how we understand our responsibility for the planet.”

There was some movement on soil protection in October 2025. The International Union for Conservation of Nature approved a resolution calling for legally binding international rules on soil.

For the researchers, this was an early sign that the issue was gaining recognition beyond the soil science community.

Work on a possible treaty is already underway at Aroura, a think tank based at the University of Sydney. Both Styc and McBratney are involved.

The group has developed an eight-stage plan that it hopes will lead to a Global Convention to Secure Soil by 2032.

The intention is not to have international authorities telling governments what to do with their land.

Instead, countries would work from a shared five-part framework. Each could adapt it to local environmental conditions and national laws while retaining control over its territory.

Nor would countries need to replace the environmental treaties they have already signed.

Until a separate soil convention comes into existence, Styc and McBratney suggest making better use of existing agreements by clarifying what responsibilities countries already have toward soil.

Public awareness matters here as well. It took years for ocean conservation to become a familiar subject outside scientific circles, and the researchers would like to see something similar happen for soil.

The 2032 goal may be difficult to achieve. The high seas treaty took nearly 20 years to negotiate.

Styc and McBratney relied on earlier research rather than conducting new experiments. Their proposed soil treaty remains untested, and it is unclear how many countries would support it.

McBratney, who was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society this year, believes soil has received far too little attention in international environmental policy.

“Soil underpins our food systems, biodiversity, water security and climate resilience, yet it remains largely invisible in international environmental governance,” said Professor McBratney.

“Through Aroura, we are working to build the scientific and policy foundations for a global convention that recognises soil as a shared responsibility.”

“We have the knowledge and the tools. What we need now is international commitment,” he said.

Without the dust arriving from Africa, the Amazon would lose one of its natural sources of phosphorus. It is a relationship that exists regardless of how people divide up the world on a map.

The authors would like international law to account for such connections when deciding how soil should be protected.

The commentary is published in the European Journal of Soil Science.

#6265. How do scientists learn from failure? This researcher has clues

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Cornell computational social scientist Yian Yin turns the tools of science on science itself. He’s studying how AI-assisted submissions are changing what gets through peer review.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Yian Yin seeks to understand the dynamics of science itself. The computational social scientist is particularly interested in how innovations happen and how they may be accelerated.

“I want to understand what the secret sources or recipes of success are,” says Yin, of Cornell University.

He applied machine learning techniques to accepted and rejected research proposals to understand how scientists learn from failures. What he found was that scientists fail, and they fail often. Some switched gears after some rejections, but others who continued their research and incorporated feedback found success at a faster rate. Those who changed ideas or scrapped original proposals did not leverage a lot from their experience.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“A group that’s not only failing better and better,” Yin says, “is also failing faster and increasingly faster towards their eventual success.”

More recently, Yin has been investigating how generative AI is changing scientific publishing. Journals are receiving more AI-assisted submissions than ever before, which is leading the peer-review process to falter. More seemingly well-written papers that lack substance are getting through, he found. Coming up with large-scale solutions requires looking at the issue in a measurable way, Yin says.

“Considering both the technological and social side of scientific ecosystems would be something that’s really beneficial for the ongoing public debate and discussion about how we accelerate science in the age of artificial intelligence,” Yin says.

#6264. Archaeologists in Kazakhstan found a tiny gold bear, and nothing like it has ever been discovered in the country

Archaeologists in Kazakhstan discovered a rare gold figurine resembling a bear in a looted Saka burial mound dating back to the Early Iron Age.

Archaeologists digging a looted burial mound in Almaty, Kazakhstan, have recovered a small cast gold figurine that they believe shows a bear.

The piece came from a Saka-period mound at the Karagaily burial ground, in the city’s Nauryzbai District. The Association of Museums of Almaty carried out the emergency excavation in 2026, and city officials announced the find on Nov. 5.

“The sculptural figurine of a bear is unique for Kazakhstan. No such finds had been discovered before,” said Lyazzat Sagyndykova, director of the association.

The burial mound measures about 82 to 85 feet (25 to 26 meters) across and stands roughly 8 feet (2.5 meters) high.

Its preliminary date is the fourth to third centuries BCE, in the Early Iron Age. That estimate rests on study of the site.

The official statement lists a robbers’ pit at 10 feet (3 meters), with no word on whether that is its depth or width.

Most of the objects inside were scattered by the looting. Fragments of Saka pottery were among the pieces recovered.

City officials describe the gold object as “presumably” a bear.

The figure sits on a plate pierced with holes. Those holes suggest the ornament was sewn onto a headdress.

Two earlier ornaments offer a comparison. A gold finial shaped like an argali, a wild mountain sheep, topped the headdress of the burial known as the Golden Man.

In 2014, a sculpted snow leopard that served the same purpose turned up at the Kok-Kainar burial ground.

“This find makes it possible to trace cultural parallels across the whole of Eurasia, from the Black Sea region to the Altai,” Sagyndykova said.

The announcement gives no height or weight for the figurine, or its position in the mound.

The excavators also found a large quantity of human bone. Presumably four adults and three children were buried there, a count that further study must confirm.

“Of particular interest is the unusually large number of human remains in a single mound,” said Marat Nurpeisov, a senior researcher at the museum group.

“As a rule, mounds of comparable size were intended for the burial of one or two people,” he added.

Anthropologists are due to examine the remains to clarify how many people were buried and in what circumstances. Research at Karagaily is continuing, Nurpeisov said.

A wider Scytho-Siberian horizon emerged in the first millennium BCE, according to the Max Planck Society. It stretched from the Altai Mountains to the Black Sea.

Its tribes shared the Scythian-Saka animal style in art. Achaemenid Iran strongly influenced how the Saka version took shape, according to UNESCO.

A genetic study released in July 2026 examined 85 Iron Age individuals from the steppe. The analysis found that people in Scythian elite burials were more closely related to one another than to lower-status people at the same sites.

That work also produced the first genome-wide data from Esik’s most famous burial, dated to 400 to 300 BCE and most likely male.

The Karagaily mound is one of many Saka kurgans around Almaty. Several of the largest groups appear on the country’s tentative World Heritage list.

The Golden Man came from Esik, about 31 miles (50 kilometers) east of Almaty, where 45 large kurgans stand. His untouched tomb held more than 4,000 gold objects, an iron sword and dagger, and a bronze mirror.

Boralday, a short distance northwest of the city, has 52 mounds. The largest is about 66 feet (20 meters) high and 492 feet (150 meters) in diameter.

Besshatyr, about 80 miles (128 kilometers) from Almaty on the right bank of the Ili River, has 81. They measure 148 to 344 feet (45 to 105 meters) across.

Silk fabrics made in China were found at Esik. UNESCO notes that such trade was under way in the fifth to fourth centuries BCE, long before the Silk Road is usually said to begin.

Almaty’s museum association has held its own excavation license since 2022. That year, in Alatau District, it opened an undisturbed warrior burial dated to the fifth to second centuries BCE.

The grave held fragments of a gold-inlaid sword, animal-style gold ornaments and silver items.

In 2024, another mound in that district yielded human bone fragments, bronze fasteners and nails. A year later, the team documented an ancient looters’ tunnel in an Early Iron Age mound.

Specialists from Italy and France have taken part in geophysical surveys at Boralday’s archaeological park.

Once the Karagaily material has been studied, the most valuable artifacts are planned for display at the Almaty Museum.

The information was obtained from the Almaty city administration.

One tooth from a cave in southern China may upend how we think about early human origins in Asia.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In a cave in southern China, archaeologists have discovered an unusual 100,000-year-old tooth that may add a brand-new branch to the human family tree. A genetic analysis of the enamel revealed that the tooth is distinct from all other examples discovered in the area and may have come from an individual who belonged to a previously unknown ancient human lineage.

In a study published Wednesday (Nov. 25) in the journal Nature, researchers described four isolated teeth recovered from two cave sites in southern China that date to around 100,000 years ago, when our extinct cousins the Denisovans roamed Asia. Teeth from one cave site are similar to Denisovans', but a tooth from the second site has a unique shape and genetic variants in the tooth enamel, suggesting it is from an "unresolved archaic Homo" group, the researchers wrote.

The teeth were recovered from archaeological cave sites named Longchuandong and Chuanshandong in the Guangxi region. Based on uranium-series dating, the two teeth from Longchuandong — a molar and a bicuspid (the teeth between the canines and molars) — date to about 104,500 to 42,600 years ago, while the two teeth from Chuanshandong — which are both bicuspids — are at least 100,800 years old.

To try to figure out which ancient human group these teeth belonged to, the researchers studied the shape and characteristics of the teeth and extracted proteins from the tooth enamel. The heritable traits of the two Longchuandong teeth lined up well with Denisovan teeth that had previously been identified, revealing that a Denisovan-related group was living in southern China in the Late Pleistocene (129,000 to 11,700 years ago), according to the study. But the Chuanshandong teeth — which the team thinks may be from the same individual — were very different.

The shape of the Chuanshandong bicuspids "did not align well with any established East Asian Homo member," the researchers wrote. For example, the Chuanshandong teeth had a complex tooth root system typically seen in Homo erectus, but they also had traits more aligned with Homo sapiens, including a more symmetrically shaped tooth crown.

The root system of the Chuanshandong tooth was complex and similar to what experts see in Homo erectus.

The researchers extracted proteins from the Longchuandong teeth and one of the Chuanshandong bicuspids and discovered they were all from chromosomally male individuals. But while the Longchuandong proteins matched those from Denisovan remains that were unearthed elsewhere in China, several of the Chuanshandong protein variants have only been identified in H. erectus and Homo antecessor, an ancient human distantly related to Neanderthals and modern humans.

The protein analysis "showed that Chuanshandong formed a sister group to the common ancestors of Neanderthals, Denisovans and H. sapiens," the researchers wrote in the study. This means that "at least two non-sapiens Homo populations may have existed in southern China's subtropics during the Middle and Late Pleistocene," they wrote.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Given the small number of 100,000-year-old fossils from China that have been analyzed to date, it is unclear what the morphology and genetics of the Chuanshandong teeth mean for our understanding of human evolution, researchers say.

Denisovans were first identified in 2010, when DNA analysis of a tiny pinkie finger bone found in a Siberian cave revealed that the group was distinct from Neanderthals and modern humans. Since then, paleoanthropologists have discovered fossils all across Asia from our extinct cousins and learned that Denisovans, Neanderthals and modern humans all interbred when they had the chance. But Denisovans' and Neanderthals' genetics are known from full genomes — the complete set of their genetic material — while due to preservation issues, most of the fossils from China have only produced proteomes, a more limited set of genetic data that provides information on the body's proteins.

The Chuanshandong proteome included an ancestral genetic variant linking them to H. erectus and H. antecessor, two groups that lived before H. sapiens arrived on the scene. The presence of these variants suggests that the Chuanshandong teeth were from someone who belonged to a primitive Homo lineage, the researchers wrote. Their unique ancient proteins could also be explained by interbreeding with H. erectus.

It's not clear whether they are our cousins.

It's too early, though, to call this a new human group, study co-author Qiaomei Fu, director of the Ancient DNA Laboratory at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, told Live Science in an email.

"We could call it the Chuanshandong group temporarily, but we need more fossil and molecular evidence to determine its affinity with other archaic Homo," Fu said. "It's not clear whether they are our cousins."

The Guangxi region of China is known for its caves, many of which have Pleistocene mammal fossils.

The new Chuanshandong proteome is extremely interesting, said John Hawks, an anthropologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who was not involved in the study. But "the paper characterizes this as an 'unknown Homo'. I wouldn't put it that way. The question is which group has variation of the proteome," he told Live Science in an email.

Hawks noted that it is currently unclear whether H. erectus or Denisovans had the specific variant identified in the Chuanshandong tooth, as paleoproteomic analysis is still a relatively new technique. If the genetic variant existed in H. erectus, then the Chuanshandong teeth, which are more similar to H. erectus in shape than they are to Neanderthals, may actually be from an H. erectus individual rather than a brand-new human group. But the comparison is further complicated by the fact that no one has yet found other Denisovan bicuspids — the type of tooth found in the Chuanshandong cave.

"I have a feeling that a comprehensive analysis with all the teeth together would be stronger than these separate papers" that Fu's research team has published recently, Hawks said. "I think there is more to learn from compiling more complete analyses."

The researchers noted in the study that excavations have been ongoing in Guangxi caves for a decade, revealing a rich variety of Pleistocene mammal fossils, including ancient human relatives. This may mean that the pace of discoveries about our species' past will soon accelerate.

"We have some new findings from this region, and we are conducting analyses on them," Fu said.

#6261. Otters nearly hunted to extinction are reappearing in Kashmir

Recent sightings of Eurasian otters in Kashmir offer hope for a species nearly wiped out locally by hunting and habitat destruction.

A video that circulated on social media in June 2025 made waves among residents of Kashmir Valley. People thought they had spotted a crocodile swimming in a local stream.

This was strange because crocodiles are not found in the valley.

The animal turned out to be a Eurasian otter, a species that once thrived in Kashmir’s rivers and wetlands.

Generations of hunting and environmental damage had nearly wiped out the local population.

Researchers Irfan Khursheed Shah and Sohail Ahmad Wagay documented the animal’s return in a study.

European travelers who visited Kashmir during the 19th century described otters as plentiful. Unfortunately, the animals were also highly prized for their thick fur.

Otter pelts fetched more than twice as much in Kashmir as they did in comparable markets elsewhere. Otter fur was even traded for gold.

The fur trade continued for decades until wildlife protection laws helped reduce commercial hunting in Kashmir.

Although the fur markets eventually disappeared, otters had already suffered a dramatic decline in numbers, bringing them close to local extinction.

Surrounded by mountains in the northwestern Himalayas, Kashmir Valley has an extensive network of freshwater habitats.

The Jhelum River runs for about 103 miles through the valley, draining an area of approximately 6,804 square miles.

Connected to the river are wetlands, lakes, streams and traditional irrigation canals known locally as kuhls. Farmers have long used these canals to grow rice.

For otters, such waterways provide feeding grounds and opportunities to move between different habitats.

Previous reports had documented otters in the neighboring Gurez, Chenab and Nelum valleys. However, evidence of their presence within Kashmir Valley itself remained scarce until the recent sightings.

In July 2025, researchers installed motion-sensitive cameras along the Rambiara and Lidder tributaries.

Although the cameras failed to capture the animals, field surveys uncovered numerous otter droppings, known as spraints.

An independent survey by a nongovernmental organization also confirmed their presence in Rambiara.

Another video from Ganderbal showed an otter eating a fish in the Sindh tributary.

Much of Kashmir has changed in the decades since otter populations declined.

Residential and commercial developments now occupy former rice fields. Some farmers have switched to growing apples, reducing the need for traditional irrigation canals.

Construction along riverbanks has also broken up natural habitats. Concrete bridges have replaced nearly all the old wooden ones.

Otters once used spaces around these wooden structures to establish their shelters, called holts, where they could rest and raise their young.

Heavy metals, pesticides and microplastics threaten the quality of freshwater habitats.

Discarded plastic bags and food packaging add to the problem. Some people also resort to destructive fishing methods involving chemicals or electric currents.

As predators that feed largely on fish, otters are particularly vulnerable to certain pollutants that accumulate in their prey.

Outside the water, the growing number of stray dogs presents another concern, particularly in populated areas.

Changing weather patterns could make life even harder for Kashmir’s returning wildlife.

Floods, mudflows and landslides can destroy otter shelters, while prolonged dry spells may leave them exposed.

Climate change could also alter the geographic distribution of Eurasian otters.

Falling water levels may reduce the availability of fish and force the animals to travel farther in search of food.

Trout farming has become a growing source of income in Kashmir. However, fish farms could become a source of tension between local communities and returning otters.

Since otters feed mainly on fish, they may find fish ponds an easy source of food.

Farmers who lose fish to otters may see the animals as pests and try to drive them away or even kill them.

One of the more unusual obstacles to otter conservation has little to do with the environment.

For years, adults in Kashmir have portrayed otters as dangerous animals to discourage children from swimming in waterways where drowning incidents occur.

Such beliefs have apparently survived across generations. In one of the recent videos, a boy could be heard saying that he would never bathe in the river again because of the otter’s presence.

In reality, otter attacks on humans are rare, although people should still keep a safe distance from wild animals.

The Eurasian otter lives across Europe, northern Africa and much of Asia. Scientists recognize 12 subspecies worldwide.

The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) classifies the species as Near Threatened due to habitat damage, fragmented populations and declining numbers of mature individuals.

The researchers recommend closer cooperation between scientists, conservation groups and government agencies in Kashmir.

Alongside habitat restoration, they suggest introducing otter mascots in schools and tourist destinations, organizing public awareness campaigns and distributing educational leaflets in local languages.

The recent sightings are promising, but whether Kashmir can support a healthy, breeding otter population remains an open question.

The full study was published in the journal Biological Diversity.

#6260. This week: Lame duck kicks off with Hegseth impeachment effort

Departing GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

The lame-duck session of Congress kicks off this week as the House is expected to consider a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth while the Senate seeks to advance a bipartisan deal on permitting reform.

Last week’s midterm elections saw Democrats claim sizable majorities in both the House and Senate in the new Congress, and among the immediate questions is whether the demoralized GOP will face attendance woes.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the expected next speaker of the House, said Sunday that he would support the Hegseth impeachment.

“I'm a hard 'yes' on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries said on ABC’s “This Week.” “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe. Pete Hegseth has got to go.”

Departing Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session.

It’s also orientation week on Capitol Hill for new members of Congress. House orientation got underway Sunday.

The Senate, meanwhile, looks to take up a bipartisan permitting bill that has the backing of President Donald Trump.

“This Landmark Permitting Reform Legislation will codify our America First Energy Agenda, and ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families, and creating High Paying American Jobs,” Trump posted on Truth Social.

Senate negotiators over the weekend released text of an amendment seeking to address remaining concerns.

“I’m grateful for the input throughout this process from Senate and House colleagues, environmental and labor organizations, and Tribal leaders. Our manager’s amendment improves [the bill] and addresses the thoughtful feedback we have received,” Senate Environment and Public Works ranking Democrat Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island said in a statement. “Now it’s time to pass this bill so we can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build big things again in America, reduce pollution, and create tons of new well-paying union jobs.”

Beyond the permitting bill, the Senate Republican majority may seek to use its remaining time trying to confirm more of Trump’s nominations before the control of the floor agenda passes to the Democrats.

"We've got the farm bill, the NDAA, and we have that third reconciliation bill that we need to get across the finish line, and there are so many things that we need to get done and buttoned up," including nominations, departing Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., said in a weekend Fox News interview. Blackburn, one of the Republicans who had success at the ballot box, is now governor-elect of Tennessee. But it's an open question how long lawmakers will want to stick around.

There’s also the matter of an imminent fight over funding the government and laying the groundwork for the new Congress. Republican leadership elections are scheduled for Tuesday, while Democratic leadership elections are expected in December. Democratic senators-elect are due on Capitol Hill Monday and Tuesday, according to the office of Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. Schumer is widely expected to be the majority leader in 2027.

There have been some calls for Senate Republicans to delay their elections, though current Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota has been widely expected to remain as the Republican leader.

“One of the things I learned in business and the Army is that after a failure, you have to start with honesty, transparency, and accountability,” Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa., said in a Sunday night statement. “As I’ve shared with Leader Thune, I don’t believe we should move to leadership elections until we have digested and debated the lessons of the midterms and how to move forward.”

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., has also been circulating a letter calling for a delay, and he has argued the election should not be held, in part, because the makeup of the Senate Republican Conference is not yet final. Senate races are still not called in Alaska and Mississippi.

Absent this week will be Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who recently had a stroke.

“The doctors are very encouraged by the progress I’ve made so far. In order to take my recovery seriously and get back to work on the quickest timeline possible, I will be spending several weeks at a rehabilitation center after being discharged from the hospital today,” Murphy said in a Friday statement.

#6259. What helps land recover after fire? This ecologist looks to the past

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Jennifer Grenz, an ecologist and member of the Lytton First Nation, asks how changes in the way people care for the land may have left it more vulnerable to wildfire.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In an increasingly fire-prone western North America, Jennifer Grenz, an ecologist and member of the Lytton First Nation, looks at fire with a holistic eye. She considers her work with landscapes recovering from catastrophic wildfire to be “deliberately unfocused,” spanning soil microbial ecology, restoration ecology, invasion biology and historical biology.

Grenz analyzes historical ecological records, like how Indigenous people have shaped and cared for ecosystems over time, to paint a comprehensive picture. “I’m interested in how those histories leave ecological legacies and hints of the stewardship of the past,” says Grenz, who leads the Indigenous Ecology Lab at the University of British Columbia in Canada. “What changed on the land that made it more vulnerable?”

Grenz spends time with many kinds of specialists, such as archaeologists, anthropologists and Indigenous elders who provide oral histories.

Moving forward, her lab will examine ecology below ground, including soil, microbial communities and root networks. The goal is to understand the role of underground ecology in critical topics like carbon sequestration, climate change, biodiversity and sustainable management.

“My motivation is in our interior Salish Territories in the southern interior of British Columbia, where my ancestors rest and where my people are,” Grenz says. “The responsibility I feel to them and to our Tmícw, which means our lands, [is] to not take us back to the past, but to show that we have the deep knowledge to help us move forward.”

#6257. Clickbait can make true information seem less believable than fake news

A study of 203 young adults found that clickbait made news seem less trustworthy, especially when the information was true.

Sensational headlines may make even accurate information seem untrustworthy. New research suggests that clickbait can undermine the credibility of a social media post, regardless of whether its content is true.

In an experiment involving 203 young adults, researchers found that accurate posts written in a sensational style received lower average truthfulness ratings than false posts written in a neutral style.

Participants were also less inclined to engage with posts featuring dramatic wording, emojis and excessive punctuation.

The volunteers were aged 18 to 31 and were recruited through the research platform Prolific.

The study was led by Michael Craig, an assistant professor of psychology at Northumbria University.

His co-authors were Kwong Him Tsang and Santosh Vijaykumar, who studies health communication.

Clickbait headlines are used by many news outlets. In a 2017 analysis cited by the team they were found in nearly 40% of unreliable outlets. About a third of mainstream outlets used them as well.

Evidence on whether clickbait increases engagement has been mixed. In one study of 1.67 million Facebook posts by media organizations more likes, shares and comments were received by clickbait.

In other studies lower engagement was reported and such headlines were judged to be of lower quality.

For the experiment 20 short posts were written by the team on five common subjects of misinformation at the time.

The topics were COVID-19 vaccines, the origin of COVID-19, climate change, cellphone radiation and the consciousness of artificial intelligence.

According to the paper, a true post and a false post were written for each topic. The researchers then made a calm version and a clickbait version of each one.

In the calm true vaccine post, readers were told that COVID-19 vaccines cannot cause COVID-19. The clickbait version of the same claim began with “The jaw-dropping lie behind COVID-19 vaccines!” and a screaming emoji.

The false posts made the opposite claims in the same two styles, the authors wrote. No source name or profile picture was shown with any post.

The researchers reported that the 20 posts were shown in a random order. Participants rated each one on a five-point scale for how likely they were to like, comment on or share it.

They also rated how truthful and credible each post seemed.

According to the paper, false posts received lower truthfulness and credibility ratings than true posts. The researchers reported that clickbait posts were also rated below calm posts and that style had the bigger effect.

In the truthfulness ratings the clickbait style cost true posts about 1.14 points on the five-point scale. False posts lost about 0.81 points when they were written as clickbait.

The team found the same result for all five topics in a further analysis. Its size was not the same for every topic.

The authors wrote that false information is likely to attract doubt based on its content alone.

The researchers suggest that false posts had less room to lose credibility because they were already viewed with suspicion.

Accurate posts started with higher ratings, leaving more room for those scores to fall.

According to the researchers the volunteers were good at telling true information from false information.

On the Misinformation Susceptibility Test, taken before the main task, about 75% of the fake headlines were identified correctly.

As the authors wrote, “Clickbait doesn’t just fail to boost engagement – it actively reduces it, while also damaging how truthful and credible a post seems.”

According to the paper, overall engagement with the posts was low. Average ratings for liking, commenting and sharing fell between “definitely not” and “probably not.”

These ratings were lowered further by the clickbait style. Participants reported that they were less likely to like, comment on or share clickbait posts than calm posts.

Again, the decrease was larger for true posts than for false posts.

“What struck us most was how self-defeating clickbait turned out to be,” the researchers wrote.

“It’s used on the assumption that it drives clicks and shares, but our participants were consistently less likely to like, comment on, or share clickbait-style posts – even when the underlying content was true.”

An idea from consumer psychology was suggested by the researchers as a possible explanation.

According to this idea, people who notice an attempt to influence them may become suspicious of the whole message.

One result differed from the others. Participants were less inclined to like or comment on false posts, but they reported similar willingness to share true and false information.

The authors wrote that this was concerning because people may share true and false content at equal rates.

Earlier research cited in the paper has linked sharing more closely to identity, social approval and emotion than to accuracy.

According to the team, efforts to reduce misinformation may need to focus on sharing decisions as well as on belief.

Everyone also filled in a news literacy questionnaire before seeing the posts. It asks people how news gets made and who has a say in it.

People who did well on it trusted clickbait less. They were also less keen to like it or comment on it. For people who did poorly, the gap between clickbait and plain posts shrank.

The headline quiz told a different story. Those more prone to believing misinformation saw less difference between true and false posts, the authors wrote.

So two separate things seem to be going on. One is spotting a pushy style. The other is judging whether a claim holds up.

The authors suggested this may be part of why clickbait is still around. It may turn off literate readers yet still reach less literate ones, who are least able to judge it.

They likened it to badly written phishing emails that may weed out careful readers, though they called this idea speculative. Teaching people about stylistic cues could help, they suggested.

According to the authors, the study recorded what people said they would do rather than what they actually did.

Real clicks and shares were not tracked, and clickbait may perform differently in platform data.

Several clickbait features were combined in each headline. For this reason the researchers could not say whether the emoji, the punctuation or the wording had the largest effect.

All of the participants were young adults living in Britain. Their political views, which may influence beliefs about several of these topics, were not measured.

The paper states that credible news outlets and public health communicators have increasingly adopted sensational styles to compete for attention.

“If credible sources such as public health bodies or scientific institutions adopt this kind of sensationalist styling to compete for attention online, our findings suggest they may be undermining the very trust they depend on, without even gaining the engagement they were hoping for,” the authors noted.

The team wrote that online safety rules should consider how content is presented and not only whether it is true.

The UK’s Online Safety Act and the European Union’s Digital Services Act were given as examples.

According to the researchers, future studies could compare what people say they would do with what they click and share.

They also suggested testing ways to reduce the harm that clickbait styling does to accurate content.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS One.

Exceptionally high tides, El Niño-fueled conditions and abnormally warm water are converging on California's coast, with authorities urging residents to limit unnecessary travel this Thanksgiving.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Major flooding of up to 2.7 feet (0.8 meters) is expected in parts of California today (Nov. 25) as record-breaking tides, El Niño-fueled conditions and warmer-than-average ocean water converge along the state's coast.

The triple flooding threat is expected to hit the San Francisco Bay Area especially hard, with San Francisco International Airport and other low-lying areas of the city bracing for deluges, while officials warned of dangerous breaking waves measuring 20 to 30 feet (6 to 9 m) tall along San Francisco's coast, the San Francisco Chronicle reported.

Meanwhile, in Southern California, coastal communities should expect potentially record-breaking "king tides" and breaking waves up to 15 feet (4.6 m) high, the National Weather Service warned on its website. King tides are exceptionally high tides that occur every year due to seasonal factors and the alignment of Earth, the sun and the moon — but this year's "super" El Niño has amplified the risk by pushing a massive "Kelvin wave" up California's coast.

Citing the forecast, several cities on California's central coast have closed beaches to shield people from hazards, including sudden waves that could wash beachgoers out to sea. Local authorities have also urged residents to limit unnecessary travel during the Thanksgiving holiday.

"As Californians head into the holiday, take a few minutes to check travel conditions, sign up for local emergency alerts, and make a plan to keep your family safe," California governor Gavin Newsom said in a statement Tuesday (Nov. 24).

The flooding comes as a perfect storm of adverse conditions has gathered on California's coastline. Scientists expected the king tides and the coastal flooding associated with them to emerge this time of the year. However, these powerful tides are now arriving on top of blistering sea temperatures due to accelerating climate change and the current El Niño event — the warm phase of a multiyear natural climate pattern that's in full swing and set to intensify through the end of the year.

Ocean water expands as it warms, swelling tides and raising the risk of strong surf and big waves. As a result, this year's tides are predicted to be at their highest levels since January 1983, when tides also coincided with El Niño-fueled storms, AFP reported.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Record-breaking “king tides,” combined with elevated surf and a large Pacific swell, are expected to bring significant coastal flooding to California during Thanksgiving week.

In January 1983, "all hell broke loose," Reinhard Flick, a researcher at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography at the University of California, San Diego, told AFP. "We had 13-foot (4-meter) waves offshore, the highest tides of the year, and hundreds of millions of dollars in damage. It hit Northern California, Southern California, everybody."

Forecasts suggest this week's conditions won't be quite that bad. But there are risks to be aware of going into winter, especially as El Niño has yet to peak and more king tides are expected in December and January.

"It could potentially be quite bad if we also have rainfall and high waves at the same time during any one of these big events, especially December and January, when rainfall generally increases on our coast," Flick said.

Sascha is a U.K.-based staff writer at Live Science. Her work has appeared in The Guardian and the health website Zoe. Besides writing, she enjoys playing tennis, bread-making and browsing second-hand shops for hidden gems.
